title: HW03 · Q10–Q11: Bitwise Operators, Shifts & Masks
text: HW03 · Q10–Q11: Bitwise Operators, Shifts & Masks Q10.1 · OR / AND / XOR Bits a 01_0110 b 11_1000 OR 0b11_1110 AND 0b01_0000 XOR 0b10_1110 Fill in OR, AND, XOR of 0b01_0110 and 0b11_1000 (comma-separated): Check OR = 0b11_1110, AND = 0b01_0000, XOR = 0b10_1110. Q10.2 · XOR as a "difference detector" XOR-ing a value with a mask flips exactly the bits that are 1 in the mask . So "what should I XOR with 0b0101 to get output X" is just X XOR 0b0101 — XOR is its own inverse. Target output Mask needed (XOR with 0b0101 ) 0b1111 0b1010 0b0101 0b0000 0b1010 0b1111 0b0000 0b0101 Fill in What to XOR with 0b0101 to get 0b1111, 0b0101, 0b1010, 0b0000 (comma-separated, in order): Check 0b1010, 0b0000, 0b1111, 0b0101. Q10.3 · Which operator does what Goal Operator Turn specific bits on | (OR) Turn specific bits off & (AND, with an inverted mask) Flip / toggle specific bits ^ (XOR) Match the goal to the operator OR turns bits on, AND turns bits off, XOR flips bits — which one flips bits? A. & B. | C. ^ Check ^ (XOR) toggles bits; | sets them on; & (with a 0-mask) clears them off. Q10.4–Q10.7 · Shifts Expression Result Why 0b0011 << 2 12 0011=3, shift left 2 = ×4 → 0b1100 = 12 0b1010 >> 1 (arithmetic, nibble) −3 1010 is negative (−6); arithmetic shift refills with the sign bit: 1101 = −3 0b1010 >>> 1 (logical, nibble) 5 logical shift always refills with 0: 0101 = 5 x << 2 shift x left by 2 bits and multiply x by 4 each left shift by 1 doubles the value; two shifts = ×4 Arithmetic right shift ( >> ) preserves sign by refilling with copies of the original MSB — it's the shift used for signed numbers. Logical right shift ( >>> ) always refills with 0s — used for unsigned numbers, where there's no sign bit to preserve. Fill in 0b0011 << 2 as a base-10 unsigned integer: Check 12. Fill in 0b1010 >> 1 (arithmetic, 4-bit) as base-10: Check −3 — sign bit (1) is copied in: 1010→1101 = −3. Fill in 0b1010 >>> 1 (logical, 4-bit) as base-10: Check 5 — zero-fill: 1010→0101 = 5. Select all that apply What does x << 2 do? A. shift x right by 2 bits B. shift x left by 2 bits C. divide x by 4 D. multiply x by 4 Check Both B and D are correct — "shift left 2" and "multiply by 4" describe the exact same operation. Q11 · Masks A byte packs several independent flags: bit0 =alive, bit1 =key, bit2 =shield, bit3 =invisible. if (player & 0b00000100) checks just the shield bit. Multiple choice What is the purpose of 0b00000100 in if (player & 0b00000100) ? It changes the player's shield status. It selects the player's shield status so the program can check it. It removes all of the player's other statuses. It checks whether any player status is active. A mask used with & inside an if is read-only — it isolates one bit so the program can test it, without touching player at all. Multiple choice Why not just write if (player) { showShield(); } ? player contains information about several different states, but we only care about the shield state. player cannot be used in an if statement. The mask converts player from binary to decimal. The mask changes the value stored in player. if (player) is true whenever any bit is set (alive OR key OR shield OR invisible) — the mask is what narrows the check down to just the shield bit. Multiple choice A robot's sensor byte: bit0 = obstacle front, bit1 = behind, bit2 = left, bit3 = right. It should turn right when there's an obstacle to its left . What belongs in if (sensors & ________) ? 0b00000001 0b00000010 0b00000100 0b00001000 "Left" is bit 2, so the mask needs exactly bit 2 set: 0b00000100 . Multiple choice A byte packs device type (bits 7–4) and device ID (bits 3–0). Extracting the ID uses data & 0b00001111 . Why are bits 7–4 of the mask 0? The programmer knows those bits of data are always zero. The programmer wants to ignore the device type when determining the ID. The programmer wants to change the device type to zero permanently. Those bits are not part of the data. AND-ing with 0 clears those bit positions in the result (without touching data itself) so only the ID bits survive into the extracted value. Multiple choice Error flags: bit0=battery, bit1=temperature, bit2=network, bit3=storage. if (errors & 0b00000101) — which description best explains the mask? Check specifically for a temperature or storage error. Check specifically for a battery or network error. Turn on the battery and network errors. Ignore the battery and network errors. 0b00000101 has bit0 (battery) and bit2 (network) set — the AND is true if either of those is set in errors . Select all that apply Using if (errors & 0b00000101) , which values of errors cause alertUser() to run? A. 0b00000000 B. 0b00000001 C. 0b00000010 D. 0b00000100 E. 0b00000101 F. 0b00001010 Check B, D, E — any value with bit0 or bit2 set produces a nonzero AND with 0b00000101 . A (all zero), C (only bit1), and F (only bits1,3) share no set bit with the mask, so their AND is 0 and the alert does not fire.

title: CL09 · Masks Recap & clear_bit
text: CL09 · Masks Recap & clear_bit A mask is a binary pattern used to select (get), set, clear, or toggle specific bits within a number. Operation Meaning Operator Select (get) read a bit's value & Set make a bit 1 | Clear make a bit 0 & with ~mask Toggle flip 0→1 or 1→0 ^ clear_bit2 : clear one fixed bit Clear bit 2 of an int8_t : build a mask that is 0 everywhere except bit 2, then invert it so it's 1 everywhere except bit 2 , and AND it in. int8_t clear_bit2(int8_t number) { int8_t mask = ~(0b100); return number & mask; } Worked example: number = 0b0000_1111 mask = ~(0b0000_0100) = 0b1111_1011 0b0000_1111 & 0b1111_1011 ------------- 0b0000_1011 Bit 2 (value 4) is gone; every other bit survives — that's exactly what AND-with-a-1-elsewhere mask guarantees. clear_bit : clear any bit i Hard-coding 0b100 only clears bit 2. To clear an arbitrary bit i , build the single-bit mask with a shift instead of a literal: 1 << i places a lone 1 at position i , then ~ flips it to all-1s-except-position- i . int8_t clear_bit(int8_t num, int8_t i) { int8_t mask = ~(1 << i); return num & mask; } Worked example: i = 5 , num = 0b1110_1010 mask = ~(1 << 5) = ~(0b0010_0000) = 0b1101_1111 0b1110_1010 & 0b1101_1111 ------------- 0b1100_1010 This is the general pattern behind every mask in this lecture: shift a 1 into place, then combine it with the number using the operator that matches what you want to do. Multiple choice Why does clear_bit use 1 << i instead of a literal like 0b100 ? Shifting is required by the C standard for masks It lets the same function clear any bit position at runtime, not just one hard-coded position Literals don't work with int8_t It makes the mask wider 1 << i places a single 1 wherever i says to, so the function generalizes from "clear bit 2" to "clear whichever bit the caller asks for." title: CL09 · update_bit : Set a Bit to an Arbitrary Value
text: CL09 · update_bit : Set a Bit to an Arbitrary Value Set/clear write a known constant (1 or 0). update_bit writes whichever value the caller passes in — it has to work for both 0 and 1 with the same code. Write update_bit(num, i, x) : set bit i of num to x (where x is 0 or 1). You can't just OR in x << i — if bit i is already 1 and x is 0, OR can never turn a 1 back into a 0. You need to clear the bit first , then set it to the requested value . int8_t update_bit(int8_t num, int8_t i, int8_t x) { int8_t mask = ~(1 << i); int8_t clear_bit_i = num & mask; // step 1: force bit i to 0 return clear_bit_i | (x << i); // step 2: OR in the new value } Two calls: update_bit(0b0101, 2, 0) and update_bit(0b0101, 1, 1) Call 1: num=0b0101, i=2, x=0 mask = ~(1<<2) = 0b1111_1011 clear_bit_i = 0b0101 & 0b1111_1011 = 0b0001 result = 0b0001 | (0<<2) = 0b0001 = 1 Call 2: num=0b0101, i=1, x=1 mask = ~(1<<1) = 0b1111_1101 clear_bit_i = 0b0101 & 0b1111_1101 = 0b0101 result = 0b0101 | (1<<1) = 0b0111 = 7 Matches the slide's expected output: 1 , then 7 . Multiple choice Why must update_bit clear bit i before ORing in x << i ? Clearing first is just a style convention, not required OR is undefined on bits that are already 1 If bit i is already 1 and x is 0, OR alone could never turn it back to 0 — only clearing first, then ORing, works for both x=0 and x=1 Clearing makes the shift faster OR can only turn bits on ; it can never turn a 1 back into a 0. Clearing first guarantees bit i starts at 0, so the following OR reliably lands whatever x actually is. True / False update_bit(num, i, x) could be written correctly as just num | (x << i) . True False False. That works only when x = 1 or bit i was already 0. If bit i is 1 and x = 0 , plain OR leaves the bit set at 1 — wrong.

title: CL09 · Performance Optimization & Bit-Packing
text: CL09 · Performance Optimization & Bit-Packing Shifting instead of multiplying/dividing Bit shifting is much more efficient than multiplying or dividing, because a shift is a single fast hardware operation while multiplication/division circuits are more complex. This is used in embedded systems, game engines, and other performance-critical code. Example: multiplying x by 4 x *= 4; // works, but goes through general multiplication x << 2; // same result, much faster — shifting left by 2 = ×4 In-class problem: using only bitwise operations and addition, write a line of C that multiplies a number n by 20. Show solution Hint: what combination of powers of 2 add up to 20? → 20 = 16 + 4 , so n × 20 = n × 16 + n × 4 . n = (n << 4) + (n << 2); n << 4 is n × 16 and n << 2 is n × 4 ; 16 + 4 = 20 . Bit-packing Bit-packing stores multiple small values (flags, booleans, short integers) into a single larger data type using shifts and bitwise OR. It's used in video encoding and file compression algorithms to avoid wasting space on values that don't need a full byte or word. In-class problem: combine two 4-bit values (nibbles) into a single uint8_t , formatted as {high_nibble, low_nibble} . Example: high_nibble = 0b0101 , low_nibble = 0b1100 → result = 0b0101_1100 Show solution uint8_t packed = (high_nibble << 4) | low_nibble; Shifting high_nibble left by 4 moves it into the top four bit positions; ORing in low_nibble (which only occupies the bottom four bits) fills in the rest without disturbing the top. Extracting color channels from a packed hex color An RGB hex color like 0x7BAFD4 ("Carolina Blue") packs three 8-bit channels into one uint32_t : red in bits 23–16, green in bits 15–8, blue in bits 7–0. Extracting a channel is shift into position, then mask off the rest — the mirror image of bit-packing. uint32_t color = 0x7BAFD4; uint32_t red = (color >> 16) & 0xFF; // 0x7B uint32_t green = (color >> 8) & 0xFF; // 0xAF uint32_t blue = color & 0xFF; // 0xD4 Isolating blue: 0x7BAFD4 & 0x0000FF = 0x0000D4 . Isolating green: shift right 8 first ( 0x7BAFD4 >> 8 = 0x007BAF ), then mask with 0xFF to drop the leftover red digits, giving 0x0000AF . Isolating red follows the same pattern with a shift of 16. Order matters: masking before shifting for green/red would leave the channel sitting at the wrong bit position instead of down at bits 7–0. For color = 0x7BAFD4 , what expression correctly isolates the green channel? > 8) & 0xFF~~~(color>>8)&0xFF"> Check True / False Bit-packing and channel-extraction are inverse operations: one combines with shift+OR, the other separates with shift+AND. True False True. Packing shifts a value into its slot and ORs it into a bigger container; extracting shifts that slot down to position 0 and ANDs with a mask to strip everything else away.

text: True / False Bit-packing and channel-extraction are inverse operations: one combines with shift+OR, the other separates with shift+AND. — True. Packing shifts a value into its slot and ORs it into a bigger container; extracting shifts that slot down to position 0 and ANDs with a mask to strip everything else away.

title: RD08 Self-Check · Bitwise Operators
text: RD08 Self-Check · Bitwise Operators Recreates the RD08 reading quiz (13 pts: Q1 is 9 pts on shifts and identities, Q2 is 4 pts on masks). Q1 · Bitwise identities & shifts (9 pts) 1.1 Which expression is always equal to n for any integer n ? n | ~n n | n + 1 n | 0b111…1 n | 0b000…0 ORing with all-zeros changes nothing — every bit of n is preserved exactly. 1.2 Which expression always evaluates to 0b000…0 ? n & 0b111…1 n & n n & ~n n & (n << 1) Every bit of n and its complement ~n disagree at every position, so ANDing them can never produce a 1 anywhere. 1.3 What is the result of n ^ n ? n ~n 0b111…1 0b000…0 XOR produces a 1 only where bits differ. A number XORed with itself has identical bits at every position, so the result is all zeros. 1.4 What is the effect of the expression x << k ? Divides x by 2^k Multiplies x by 2^k (if no overflow) Shifts bits right and fills with zeros Toggles the lowest k bits Left shift moves every bit up k positions, which is equivalent to multiplying by 2^k as long as no significant bits fall off the top. 1.5 Logical right shift is typically used for: Signed integers only Unsigned integers Floating-point values Characters only Logical right shift always fills with 0s — correct for unsigned values, which have no sign bit to preserve. 1.6 Arithmetic right shift differs from logical right shift because it: Fills left bits with 1s only Fills left bits with 0s only Reverses the bits Preserves the sign bit Arithmetic right shift copies the original leftmost (sign) bit into the vacated positions — 0s for a positive number, 1s for a negative one — so the sign is preserved either way. 1.7 Which statement is correct in C? Signed right shift is always arithmetic. Unsigned right shift is always arithmetic. Unsigned right shift is logical; signed right shift is implementation-defined. Both signed and unsigned right shifts are logical. The C standard guarantees unsigned >> is logical, but leaves the behavior of >> on negative signed values up to the implementation (in practice, almost always arithmetic on real compilers/hardware). 1.8 uint8_t b = 2; printf("%d\\n", b >> 1); — what is printed? 0 1 2 4 0b0000_0010 >> 1 = 0b0000_0001 = 1 . Unsigned, so this is a logical shift regardless. 1.9 int8_t x = -5; with arithmetic right shift — what is x >> 1 ? -2 -3 -4 125 -5 is 0b1111_1011 . Arithmetic right shift by 1 copies the sign bit in: 0b1111_1101 = -3 . (Right-shifting a negative number rounds toward negative infinity, not toward zero — so this is -3, not -2.) Q2 · Masks (4 pts) 2.1 What is a bit mask used for? Encrypting data Increasing performance of multiplication Converting decimal to binary Selecting, setting, clearing, or toggling specific bits That's the definition from the reading — a mask is a binary pattern used for exactly those four operations. 2.2 Which expression correctly checks whether bit i of num is set? num & (1 << i) num | (1 << i) num ^ (1 << i) ~num & (1 << i) ANDing with a single-bit mask leaves only bit i 's value in the result (nonzero means it was set, zero means it was clear). 2.3 Which expression sets bit i of num to 1? num & (1 << i) num ^ (1 << i) num | (1 << i) num >> i OR forces bit i to 1 while leaving every other bit untouched ( x|0=x , x|1=1 ). 2.4 Which operation clears bit i (sets it to 0)? num | ~(1 << i) num & ~(1 << i) num ^ ~(1 << i) num << ~(1 << i) AND with a mask that is 0 only at position i (everywhere else 1) is exactly clear_bit from this lecture.

title: CL10 · Breakpoints, Stepping & the Watch Panel
text: CL10 · Breakpoints, Stepping & the Watch Panel A debugger lets you pause a running program and inspect its state, instead of guessing from printf output alone. VS Code's debugger for C is GDB , driven through the Microsoft C/C++ extension. Breakpoints Click in the gutter (the strip to the left of the line numbers) to drop a breakpoint — a red dot appears. When you launch the debugger, execution runs normally until it reaches that line, then pauses before that line executes. #include <stdio.h> int main() { int my_char; ● while ((my_char = getchar()) != EOF) { <- breakpoint here if (my_char >= 'a' && my_char <= 'z') { my_char = my_char - ('a' - 'A'); } putchar(my_char); fflush(stdout); } } Launching & stepping Click the debug button in the upper-right, then choose Debug active file . Once paused at a breakpoint, the stepping toolbar controls execution one line (or one function) at a time. Step Over Step Into Definition Executes the current line completely but skips stepping into any functions it calls. Executes the current line and pauses inside any function it calls. Use case You don't care about a function's internals — just move to the next line of the current function. You want to examine what's happening inside the called function. What happens If the line calls a function, that function runs to completion in one jump. The debugger pauses at the first line inside the callee; you can step through it line by line. On the demo program's getchar() line, step-over and step-into behave the same way in practice, since there's no interesting internal logic to inspect inside getchar . Reading variables — the Variables and Watch panels The Variables panel (left side) shows local variables live as you step. A variable declared int is shown in decimal , even if it's conceptually holding a character — after getchar() reads 'a' , the panel shows c = 97 , not 'a' . To see a variable's char interpretation, add a watch expression : open the Watch panel (just below Variables), click + , and type a cast like (char)c . A watchpoint lets you monitor a specific variable or memory location as the program runs, and casting is how you re-interpret the same bits in a more useful type. WATCH (char)c = 97 'a' As you keep stepping, watch this same expression update: after the code uppercases it, (char)c becomes 65 'A' ; on the next loop iteration reading a newline, it becomes 10 '\\n' . Multiple choice Why does the Variables panel show c = 97 instead of c = 'a' after reading a lowercase 'a'? The debugger made a mistake c is declared as int , so the panel displays it in decimal — the same bits interpreted as a different type 'a' can't be stored in a variable Only char -typed variables show numeric values The debugger displays a variable according to its declared type. Since c was declared int , its bits are shown as a decimal integer — a watch expression that casts to char is what re-interprets those same bits as an ASCII character. True / False Step Over and Step Into always behave differently, no matter what line you're stepping from. True False False. They only diverge when the current line calls a function. On a line with no function call (or a call with nothing interesting to inspect inside), both do the same thing.

title: CL10 · Input/Output Buffering & fflush
text: CL10 · Input/Output Buffering & fflush Terminal I/O is buffered — data doesn't move character-by-character between your program and the terminal. It sits in memory until something forces it through. Input buffering Input from stdin is stored in a buffer before it's handed to your program. When you type at the terminal, nothing reaches your program until: you press Enter , or the buffer fills up. This is why, when stepping through getchar() , the program appears to "hang" waiting on the terminal — it isn't stuck, it's genuinely waiting for you to press Enter before the buffer flushes and getchar() can return the first character. Output buffering Text you send with printf (or putchar ) is also stored temporarily in a buffer, and only actually sent to the terminal — flushed — when: a newline character ( \\n ) is encountered, the buffer fills up, or the program explicitly flushes it with fflush(stdout) . Example: the buffer can be holding "Apples\\n" internally before it's ever written out — the newline is what triggers the flush. Why the demo program calls fflush(stdout) every iteration printf / putchar use buffered I/O — text is stored internally and only sent to the terminal when the buffer is flushed (newline, full buffer, or program exit). If you don't call fflush(stdout) while debugging, you may not see your program's output immediately as you step through the code, which makes it much harder to observe intermediate states one character at a time. Calling fflush(stdout) forces the buffer out right away, so each character appears the moment it's produced. title: CL10 · launch.json & tasks.json
text: CL10 · launch.json & tasks.json These are both hidden files (name starts with . , like .vscode , .git , .gitignore , .bashrc ) — not shown by a normal directory listing, used for configuration and metadata you don't usually touch directly. tasks.json — how the build happens Before the debugger configuration starts, VS Code runs the task named by "preLaunchTask": "build" , which is defined in .vscode/tasks.json : "command": "gcc", "args": [ "-fdiagnostics-color=always", "-g", "-Wall", "-Wextra", "-Wpedantic", "\${file}", "-o", "\${fileDirname}/\${fileBasenameNoExtension}" ] Variable Meaning \${file} the currently active file in VS Code \${fileDirname} the directory containing the active file \${fileBasenameNoExtension} the active file's name, without its extension For active file /home/student/project/main.c , this expands to: gcc -fdiagnostics-color=always -g -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic \\ /home/student/project/main.c -o /home/student/project/main The executable takes the source file's base name — main.c produces main . launch.json — how the debugger runs it After the build finishes, VS Code reads .vscode/launch.json to decide how to actually run the program under the debugger. Field Meaning "type": "cppdbg" use Microsoft's C/C++ extension as the debug adapter for this configuration "MIMode": "gdb" the debug adapter should talk to GDB — "MI" stands for Machine Interface, GDB's programmatic control interface "preLaunchTask": "build" run the build task from tasks.json first Layering, top to bottom: VS Code (the UI you interact with) → cppdbg (the middle-layer debug adapter) → GDB (the program actually doing the debugging). GDB is the thing actually debugging your program; VS Code and cppdbg are the interface that lets you control it. Two debug configurations: plain vs. redirected input Debug active file launches the compiled executable directly: "program": "\${fileDirname}/\${fileBasenameNoExtension}" Debug with input redirected works differently — instead of launching the program directly, it launches Bash and hands Bash a command to run: "program": "/bin/bash", "args": [ "-lc", "\\"\${fileDirname}/\${fileBasenameNoExtension}\\" < \\"\${fileDirname}/test\\"" ] After variable substitution, that's effectively: /home/student/project/main < /home/student/project/test which runs the program with stdin redirected from the file test , instead of reading from the interactive terminal. To read from a different file, or one in a subdirectory, just edit the path after < in args — e.g. \${fileDirname}/example.in or \${fileDirname}/one_dir/two_dir/new_example . Flag Meaning -c execute the command that follows, then exit (rather than starting an interactive shell that waits for typed commands) -l behave as a login shell , which affects which shell startup files/environment get loaded Multiple choice What does "Debug with input redirected" actually launch under the debugger? The compiled executable directly, same as "Debug active file" GDB in a special redirected mode /bin/bash , given a -c command that runs the executable with < redirection from a file A Python wrapper script It launches Bash with -lc "<program> < <file>" — Bash performs the redirection, then runs your program with stdin already pointed at the file. True / False tasks.json controls how the program is built, while launch.json controls how it's run under the debugger. True False True. tasks.json defines the build task (the gcc invocation); launch.json 's preLaunchTask field is what wires that build to run automatically before each debug session starts.

title: CL10 · The Debugging Process (worked example)
text: CL10 · The Debugging Process (worked example) Buggy function — meant to set bit 3, toggle bit 2, clear bit 1, and set bit 0: int modifyBits(int x) { // Step 1: Set bit 3 x = x | (1 << 3); // Step 2: Toggle bit 2 x = x ^ (1 << 2); // Step 3: Clear bit 1 // BUG: XOR toggles instead of clears x = x ^ (1 << 1); // Step 4: Set bit 0 x = x | 1; return x; } int main(void) { int result; result = modifyBits(2); printf("Test 1: expected 13, got %d\\n", result); result = modifyBits(6); printf("Test 2: expected 9, got %d\\n", result); result = modifyBits(0); printf("Test 3: expected 13, got %d\\n", result); return 0; } Step 1 · Run the tests to see which one fails modifyBits(2) : x=0b010 starts with bit 1 already set. Step 3's x ^ (1<<1) toggles bit 1 — since it's already 1, XOR flips it to 0, which is what the test happens to expect. Same story for modifyBits(6) : bit 1 of 6 = 0b110 starts at 1, so toggling it also happens to clear it. But modifyBits(0) starts with bit 1 already 0 — toggling a 0 sets it to 1 instead of leaving it clear. Test 3 fails. Step 2 · Predict, then compare against actual Operation Prediction Initial value of num 0x0 = 0b0000_0000 Set bit 3 0x8 = 0b0000_1000 Toggle bit 2 0xC = 0b0000_1100 Clear bit 1 (intended) 0xC = 0b0000_1100 — unchanged, bit 1 was already 0 Set bit 0 0xD = 0b0000_1101 Set a breakpoint at the start of the failing test, and watch num (or x ) — ideally in hex, since bit patterns are far more readable as hex than decimal. Step through line by line and find exactly where the actual value stops matching the prediction. Step 3 · Where it diverges Stepping past the "Clear bit 1" line with x = 0b0000_1100 : x ^ (1<<1) XORs in 0b0000_0010 . Since bit 1 of x is currently 0, XOR flips it to 1 instead of leaving it at 0 — giving 0b0000_1110 , which does not match the 0b0000_1100 prediction. That's the exact line where behavior departs from intent. Step 4 · Fix "Clear" should use AND with an inverted mask, not XOR: x = x & ~(1 << 1); // correctly clears bit 1 regardless of its current value Multiple choice Why does modifyBits(2) pass even though the "clear bit 1" line is buggy? Bit 1 of the input happens to already be 1, so toggling it with XOR happens to produce the same result that clearing it would The test comparison is wrong XOR and AND are interchangeable for clearing bits The bug only affects bit 0 This is exactly why writing multiple test cases with different inputs matters — a bug that toggles instead of clears is invisible on inputs where the bit was already 1, and only shows up once you test an input where it starts at 0. title: CL11 · Shell Prompt Configuration
text: CL11 · Shell Prompt Configuration CLI, Terminal, Shell — quick recap CLI (Command Line Interface): a text-based way to interact with a computer, typing commands instead of clicking. Terminal: the program/window that lets you type commands and see output. Shell: the program that actually interprets and runs your commands (Bash is the shell used in this course). Written instructions often show a $ at the start of a line to represent the shell prompt — you don't type the $ itself, just what comes after it. PS1 — the prompt variable PS1 is the environment variable that controls what your shell prompt looks like. You can build a custom prompt out of format specifiers: Specifier Meaning %n Username @ Literal "at" separator %m Hostname (machine name) %1~ Current directory (abbreviated to the last component) %# A prompt symbol that differs for a regular user vs. root Bash's own PS1 syntax uses specifiers like \\u (user), \\h (host), and \\w (working directory) — different characters, same underlying idea: a variable that controls what gets displayed before every command. Multiple choice The $ shown at the start of a line in course instructions means: Part of the command you must type A special Bash variable The shell prompt — don't type it A syntax error marker The $ just represents the prompt so instructions read naturally; only what follows it should actually be typed.

title: CL11 · Environment Variables
text: CL11 · Environment Variables What's an environment variable? An environment variable is a named piece of data stored by the shell that programs (including child processes) can read. Example: export COURSE="COMP 211" This creates (or promotes) a variable named COURSE and marks it as an environment variable, meaning it's passed along to any child processes the shell starts. Common environment variables Variable Holds PATH Directories the shell searches for executables HOME Your home directory USER Your username SHELL Path to your default shell (e.g. /bin/bash ) OLDPWD The previous working directory (before your last cd ) PS1 Your prompt format string View them all with printenv or env . View one with echo "$VAR" . $VAR vs. ${VAR} vs. bare VAR Form Meaning VAR Just the literal text "VAR" — not expanded $VAR Expands to the variable's value \${VAR} Same expansion, but with explicit boundaries — needed when the variable name is immediately followed by more text, e.g. \${VAR}suffix (without braces, Bash would try to expand a variable literally named VARsuffix ). Setting, exporting, modifying, unsetting Assign a shell variable (no spaces around = ): VAR=value . Only visible in the current shell, not in child processes. Promote it to an environment variable: export VAR (or combine: export VAR=value ). Now child shells/processes can see it too. Modify an existing variable (append to it): export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/bin" — the old value is referenced with $PATH so nothing is lost. Remove a variable: unset VAR . Child shells & what they inherit Running bash from inside a shell starts a child shell . A child shell inherits environment variables (anything export ed) from its parent, but does not inherit plain shell variables that were never exported. Use exit to leave the child shell and return to the parent. In the parent shell: export COURSE="COMP 211" EDITOR=nano bash # start a child shell In the child shell: echo "$COURSE" # -> COMP 211 (inherited, exported) echo "$EDITOR" # -> (empty, never exported) exit # back to parent COURSE was exported, so the child shell can see it. EDITOR was only ever a plain shell variable in the parent (never exported), so the child shell has no idea it exists. To make a shell variable visible to child processes, you must ______ it. Check

title: CL11 · $PATH
text: CL11 · $PATH What $PATH is for $PATH is a colon-separated list of directories. When you type a command name (not a path), the shell searches each directory in $PATH , in order , and runs the first matching executable it finds. A typical Linux $PATH : /usr/bin:/bin Directory Purpose Examples /usr/bin Many standard system commands gcc , python3 , git /bin Essential system commands ls , cp , mv , cat , mkdir , pwd , rm The which command tells you which executable would actually run: which python3 → /usr/bin/python3 . Worked example: which hello runs? You're in /home/student/project , and $PATH is /home/student/bin:/usr/bin:/bin . There's a hello executable in /usr/bin , in /home/student/bin , and in the current directory. Command Which hello runs? ./hello /home/student/project/hello — explicit relative path, no $PATH search /usr/bin/hello /usr/bin/hello — explicit absolute path ../bin/hello /home/student/bin/hello — explicit relative path hello /home/student/bin/hello — bare name, so $PATH is searched in order , and /home/student/bin comes first Key idea: giving any kind of path ( ./ , ../ , or an absolute path starting with / ) skips the $PATH search entirely. Only a bare command name triggers a $PATH search. Modifying $PATH — order matters, and don't nuke it Add to the front (higher priority): export PATH="/home/student/bin:$PATH" Now /home/student/bin is searched first. Add to the end (lower priority): export PATH="$PATH:/home/student/bin" Existing directories are searched first; /home/student/bin is the fallback. Careful: export PATH="/home/student/bin" (no $PATH on the right side) replaces the entire PATH, which can break basic commands like ls , cat , and grep because the shell can no longer find them! Worked example: building a new $PATH Suppose $PATH is /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin and you run: export PATH="/home/student/bin:$PATH" The new value of $PATH is: Show answer /home/student/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin Worked example: braces needed Current PATH: /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin , home directory: /home/student . You run: export PATH="\${PATH}:\${HOME}/mybin" New value of $PATH : Show answer /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/home/student/mybin Pipeline example: which programs use $PATH? Given the pipeline: ./producer | sort | ./consumer | wc -l Command Search $PATH or use specified path? ./producer Specified path (starts with ./ ) sort Search $PATH (bare name) ./consumer Specified path (starts with ./ ) wc Search $PATH (bare name) Temporary vs. persistent $PATH changes export PATH="$PATH:/home/student/bin" only changes the current shell session . Verify it with echo $PATH . Close the terminal and open a new one, and the change is gone . To make it permanent, put the export command in your ~/.bashrc (next topic).

title: CL11 · .bashrc, Aliases & RD10
text: CL11 · .bashrc, Aliases & RD10 What is .bashrc ? ~/.bashrc is a configuration file for Bash . It's not just a list of settings — it literally contains Bash commands that get executed every time you start a new interactive Bash shell. Located in your home directory : ~/.bashrc . The leading . makes it a hidden file — it won't show up with a plain ls . See it with ls -a ~ . Bash startup sequence Start Bash → Read ~/.bashrc → Execute the commands in .bashrc → Display your prompt → Wait for you to enter commands. This is why anything you put in .bashrc — a custom PS1 , an export , an alias — is automatically in effect every time you open a new terminal. A typical .bashrc # Change the prompt PS1="learncli$ " # Create a shortcut alias ll="ls -al" # Set an environment variable export EDITOR="vim" # Add a directory containing programs to PATH export PATH="\${PATH}:\${HOME}/bin" source — reloading without a new shell If you edit .bashrc while a shell is already running, the change generally won't affect that already-running shell (it only re-reads .bashrc at startup). You have two options: Close the terminal and open a new one, or Tell the current shell to re-read the file: source ~/.bashrc The source command tells Bash to read a file and execute the commands in it in the current shell (rather than in a new child process). You've likely used this before: activating a Python virtual environment is exactly this pattern — source .venv/bin/activate runs a shell script that modifies your current shell's $PATH (and prompt) so that python / pip point inside .venv instead of the system Python. That's also why activating a venv has to be done with source (or the shorthand . ) rather than just running the script directly — running it normally would modify a child shell's environment, which disappears the instant that child shell exits. Alias An alias creates a shortcut for a shell command: alias ll='ls -al' alias c='clear' After adding these (and reloading, e.g. via source ~/.bashrc ), typing ll runs ls -al , and typing c clears the terminal. A very common safety alias: alias rm='rm -i' This makes plain rm somefile prompt you to confirm before deleting — it doesn't rename anything or block rm outright, it just adds the -i (interactive/confirm) option automatically. RD10 self-check — Dot Files & .bashrc Questions mirror the actual graded RD10 reading quiz (Dive Into Systems §17.14). 1.1 What is the primary purpose of dot files, such as .bashrc and .vimrc ? To store deleted files To configure the behavior of applications To store executable programs To prevent users from accessing files Dot files like .bashrc and .vimrc hold configuration/settings for an application or shell. 1.1 A student edits their .bashrc file, but the changes do not appear in their currently running Bash shell. What could they do to apply the changes? ls -a source ~/.bashrc which .bashrc env .bashrc source re-reads and executes the file in the current shell, applying the change immediately without opening a new terminal. 1.1 What does the env command display? All environment variables All hidden files All executable programs All command aliases env (and printenv ) lists every environment variable currently set. 1.1 Which command can you use to determine which version of gcc will be executed? where gcc echo gcc which gcc path gcc which searches $PATH and reports the exact executable that would run. 1.2 Which command displays the current value of the PATH environment variable? env PATH which PATH echo $PATH ls $PATH $ expands the variable so echo can print its value. 1.2 What is the purpose of the PATH environment variable? It specifies the current working directory It lists directories where the shell should search for programs It specifies where hidden files are stored It stores the full path of every file on the system The shell walks these directories, in order, looking for a matching executable. 1.2 Consider: PATH=$PATH:/home/sarita/mybin . What does it do? Replaces the existing PATH with /home/sarita/mybin Adds /home/sarita/mybin to the beginning of PATH Adds /home/sarita/mybin to the end of the existing PATH Changes the current directory to /home/sarita/mybin Putting $PATH first preserves the old value; the new directory is appended after it, so it's searched last. 1.2 Why might a user add a directory containing their own programs to PATH? So the programs become hidden So the programs can be run without typing their full path So Bash automatically compiles the programs So the programs cannot be deleted Once its directory is on PATH, a bare command name is enough — no ./ or full path needed. 1.2 A user's PATH is /usr/bin:/bin:/home/alex/mybin . There's a program named testprog in both /bin and /home/alex/mybin . Which version runs when the user types testprog ? /home/alex/mybin/testprog /bin/testprog Both programs Whichever was created most recently The shell searches PATH left to right and stops at the first match; /bin comes before /home/alex/mybin . 1.3 What is the purpose of a Bash alias? To rename a file To create another user account To provide shorthand for a command or automatically add options to it To add a directory to PATH An alias is a text substitution the shell performs before running the command. 1.3 Given alias rm="rm -i" in .bashrc, what happens when the user enters rm notes ? notes is immediately deleted Bash refuses to run rm The user is prompted to confirm before notes is removed The file is renamed to notes-i The alias expands rm notes into rm -i notes , adding the interactive/confirm flag. 1.3 Sam adds alias gt31="cd ~/classes/CS31" to .bashrc. After the alias is loaded, what does entering gt31 do? Lists the contents of the CS31 directory Changes the current directory to ~/classes/CS31 Adds CS31 to PATH Creates a directory named gt31 The alias is just shorthand for the literal cd ~/classes/CS31 command.

title: CL12 · Character Arrays: sizeof vs. strlen
text: CL12 · Character Arrays: sizeof vs. strlen The program char str1[] = "211"; char str2[] = "U\\nN\\nC\\n"; char str3[] = "She said \\"hello\\"!"; char str4[25] = {'U','N','C','\\n','t','a','\\0','r','h','e','e','l','s','\\0'}; char dest[20]; strcpy(dest, str1); sizeof reports the total allocated size of the array (including the null terminator and any unused space); strlen reports the length of the string up to (not including) the first '\\0' , regardless of how much space is actually allocated. Fill in the program output Variable sizeof strlen Why str1 4 3 "211" + implicit \\0 = 4 bytes; 3 visible chars str2 7 6 Each \\n is one char: U,\\n,N,\\n,C,\\n + \\0 = 7 bytes, 6 visible chars str3 18 17 Escaped quotes \\" are one char each; count every char + \\0 str4 25 6 Array declared with a fixed size of 25, but the FIRST \\0 appears after just 6 characters (U,N,C,\\n,t,a) — strlen stops there even though more data follows in the array dest 20 3 Declared as char dest[20]; strcpy copied "211" (3 chars + \\0) into it Key takeaway: sizeof is a compile-time property of the array's declared size; strlen is a runtime scan that stops at the first null byte, no matter how the array itself is sized. Printed output What do the four printf("%s", ...) calls followed by printf("\\nEnd\\n") print? Show answer 211U N C She said "hello"!UNC ta End Each %s print stops at the first '\\0' it hits — note how str2's embedded \\n s actually produce newlines when printed, and str4 prints only up through ta (its first null terminator) even though "rhee ls" is still sitting in the array afterward, unreachable by %s . Why does str4 's strlen (6) not match its declared size (25)? Check

title: CL12 · Bitwise Practice: Image Filters
text: CL12 · Bitwise Practice: Image Filters The problem Write uint32_t warm_filter(uint32_t hex_color) that takes a 24-bit RGB color packed into a 32-bit int (format 0xRRGGBB ) and returns a "warmed" version: add 0x20 to the red channel, clamped at 0xFF , and leave green/blue unchanged. 4-step skeleton: Extract the current red channel: uint32_t red = (hex_color >> 16) & 0xFF; Increase it, clamped at 0xFF: uint32_t new_red = (red + 0x20 > 0xFF) ? 0xFF : red + 0x20; Clear the original red bits: uint32_t cleared = hex_color & 0x00FFFFFF; Insert the new red value: return cleared | (new_red << 16); Worked examples Input Output Why 0x123456 0x323456 Red 0x12 + 0x20 = 0x32, no clamping needed 0xF0ABCD 0xFFABCD Red 0xF0 + 0x20 = 0x110, which overflows 0xFF, so it clamps to 0xFF Multiple choice Why is step 3 (clearing the original red bits) necessary before OR-ing in the new red value? It isn't — you could skip it OR-ing a new value into bits that already hold 1s can't turn those bits back to 0, so the old red bits must be cleared first It converts the number from signed to unsigned It's needed to prevent integer overflow This is the same clear-then-set pattern from update_bit : OR can only turn bits on, so any old 1-bits in that field have to be zeroed out first, or they'd "leak through" into the result.

title: CL12 · Stack Diagram Practice
text: CL12 · Stack Diagram Practice The program void update(int32_t arr[], int64_t value) { value = value * 2; for (int8_t i = 0; i < ARR_SIZE; i += 3) { arr[i] = value * 2; } } int main(void) { int64_t x = 5; int32_t a[ARR_SIZE] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}; update(a, x); return 0; } Assume ARR_SIZE is 5. Just before update returns, what has happened to x in main , and to the array? Draw the stack and find where the stack pointer sits. Show answer x in main is unchanged (still 5). Arguments in C are passed by value : update receives its own local copy of value (initialized from x ). Reassigning value = value * 2; inside update only modifies that function's own stack frame — it has no effect on the caller's x . The array is different: arr is a pointer to the same memory as a in main (arrays decay to pointers when passed to functions), so writes through arr[i] do modify a in main . With value now 10 inside update , the loop runs for i = 0 and i = 3 (since i += 3 and the loop stops once i >= ARR_SIZE ), setting a[0] = 20 and a[3] = 20 . So just before update returns: a = {20, 2, 3, 20, 5} , and the stack pointer sits inside update 's frame, which sits above main 's frame — the stack grows downward and update was called more recently, so its frame is at a lower address, closer to the current top of the stack. True/False Because value is reassigned inside update , x in main also changes. True False False — value is a separate, local copy. Only pointer/array parameters let a callee modify the caller's data.

The real checkoff will have the same style and skill coverage but different specifics — a different program, different variable names and values, a different bug. So the goal is fluency with the debugger : knowing which button or command answers a spoken prompt on sight , and being able to say why out loud. Format What that means When & where One-on-one with a TA in the 211 office-hour room (SN143) , Mon Sep 28 – Fri Oct 2 . Check in When you arrive, submit a ticket on the CSXL queue (csxl.unc.edu/course/215/office-hours): type Assignment Help , and put your name and scheduled appointment time in the description. Time About 15 minutes on average, inside a 30-minute slot . If you aren't finished when the slot ends, you're graded on what you've done by then. Sign-up & practice The sign-up deadline was Fri Sep 25, 11:59pm and the optional practice sessions were Thu Sep 24 — both have already passed. If you don't have a slot yet, ask the course staff right away. Get the debugger working before you walk in. The handout is blunt about this: if your debugger isn't set up when your slot starts, you get no extra time — the setup comes out of your own 30 minutes, and it is very hard to finish the checkoff while also fixing VS Code. Use the checklist below tonight. You can clone a repo git clone https://github.com/COMP211-FA26/debugging-checkoff-practice — the released sample repo; it contains practice.c and its .vscode folder. The C/C++ extension is installed and gdb exists Open practice.c , click the gutter to drop a red breakpoint, then press the debug button → Debug active file . It must actually pause on your breakpoint. Both debug configurations appear In the debug dropdown you should see Debug active file and Debug with input redirected . If the second one is missing, look at .vscode/launch.json . You know where the panes are Variables , Watch , Call Stack , Breakpoints , and the Debug Console tab. You can compile from the terminal gcc practice.c -o yourname , then ./yourname . .vscode is a hidden folder (leading dot) — use ls -a if you can't find it in the terminal, and see CL10 · launch.json & tasks.json for what's inside. Items marked not in the sample are on the official list but never came up in the sample checkoff's ten sections — so they're the ones most likely to surprise you, and the Drill tab tests them on purpose. title: Walkthrough · Worked Through the Sample Checkoff's 10 Sections
text: Walkthrough · Worked Through the Sample Checkoff's 10 Sections The sample program ( practice.c ) is an order processor : main → process_order() → calculate_item_total() . It reads a discount with scanf , upper-cases an order_code , and sums an array prices[] . Answers below come from the released solution key; the “why” is what transfers to a checkoff with a different program. Each section ends with a Say it aloud line, because the TA will ask you to explain, not just click. Debugger controls at a glance Command What it does Default VS Code key Continue Run until the next breakpoint (or the program ends) F5 Step Over Run the current line fully; if it calls a function, run that function to completion without entering it F10 Step Into Run the current line, and if it calls a function, pause on that function's first line F11 Step Out Finish the current function and pause back in the function that called it Shift + F11 Restart Stop and relaunch from the beginning Ctrl + Shift + F5 On a Mac laptop you may need to hold fn for the F-keys — and the checkoff says “ verbally state: step over ,” so learn the names , not just the buttons. The toolbar's icons have hover labels if you blank. 1 · Run the program Task Answer Compile, naming the executable <student_name> gcc practice.c -o cece (with your own name instead of cece ) Run normally ./cece , then type 8 at the prompt What happened to order_code ? ord-a7 becomes ORD-A7 Compile-and-run is the same skill as Checkoff 1: the name goes immediately after -o , and ./ is required because the current directory isn't on $PATH . “Based on the code and output” means: don't just eyeball the output — find the loop in the source that changes each character (it's the toupper pattern) and point at it . Say it aloud: “ order_code starts lowercase and the code upper-cases it in place, so the output shows ORD-A7 .” 2 · Regular breakpoint Task Answer Where's the breakpoint? On total += prices[i]; inside the loop of calculate_item_total() — click the gutter left of the line number At the first stop: i 0 — read it in the Variables pane prices[i] 18 — not a plain variable, so type it in the Watch pane or Debug Console total 0 — Variables pane Already added, or about to be? About to be. The highlighted line is the one that hasn't executed yet. Press Continue — where does it stop? The same line, next iteration (so i = 1 and total = 18 ) A breakpoint pauses before its line runs. This is the single most-tested idea in the checkoff. The highlighted line is “what will happen next,” not “what just happened.” That's why total is still 0 while prices[i] is already 18: the += is queued up, not done. Also notice where each value lives: variables that exist as plain locals show in Variables ; an expression like prices[i] needs Watch or the Debug Console. Say it aloud: “The line is highlighted but not executed yet — that's how I can tell the current price hasn't been added.” 3 · Conditional breakpoint Task Answer Only stop when the price is over 40 Right-click the red dot → Edit Breakpoint… → choose Expression → prices[i] > 40 → Enter Press Continue — i and prices[i] ? i = 3 , prices[i] = 46 The expression is plain C — no if keyword — and the debugger evaluates it every time it reaches that line , pausing only when it's true. Because you jumped straight to i = 3 , items 1 and 2 must both be ≤ 40 (indeed their prices add to 41, which the numbers in section 4 confirm). This is how you avoid pressing Continue 200 times in a big loop. Say it aloud: “I gave the breakpoint a condition, so it only pauses when prices[i] > 40 is true.” 4 · Debug Console Task What to type Result Current total total 59 What total will be after adding the current price (without executing) total + prices[i] 105 (59 + 46) Is the current price > 40? prices[i] > 40 true (C prints it as 1 ) Did any of that change the running program? — No The Debug Console lets you ask questions of a paused program . Reading a variable or computing total + prices[i] only looks — nothing in the program changes. That second one is the checkoff's trick question: you can preview the result of a statement without running it by writing the arithmetic yourself. (Contrast: typing an assignment such as total = 0 or total++ into the console would change the running program's state — so the answer to “did it change anything” is “no” only because these were read-only expressions.) Say it aloud: “I added the two values in the console instead of stepping, so I got 105 without touching the program.” 5–7 · Step Over, Step Into, Step Out Task Answer 5. Breakpoint on line 47, int subtotal = calculate_item_total(prices, count); . Run the call but don't follow it inside . Step Over Where will the debugger be afterwards? The line after the call — the key says line 49 (the next executable line after the call; blank lines and comments are skipped) 6. You suspect the bug is inside calculate_item_total() . Step Into → you're now in calculate_item_total How is that different from Step Over? You can now step through the function line by line; Step Over ran the whole function in one jump 7. Enough iterations — finish this function and return to the caller. Step Out Which function do you expect to land in? process_order() — the one that called it Why is Step Out useful in a larger program? You can skip the rest of a function you've decided is fine, without stepping through every remaining line/iteration or placing another breakpoint Step Over vs. Step Into matter only on a line that calls a function. On a plain assignment they behave identically. Step Out is the escape hatch after you've gone in too deep. Two details to be ready for: (1) predict before you press — the TA wants your prediction spoken first, then you verify it; (2) after a Step Out you usually land back on the call line , because the assignment ( int subtotal = … ) hasn't finished yet — the returned value is computed but not stored. One more Step Over completes it. Handout typo: section 5c says calculate_order_total() , but the function on line 47 is calculate_item_total() . If the wording confuses you in the real checkoff, ask which function they mean — don't guess. Step Into won't enter library functions like printf or toupper (no source available) — it behaves like Step Over. Only your own functions can be stepped into. Say it aloud: “I'll Step Over because I trust that function and just want its result; I'll Step Into when I suspect the bug is inside it; and Step Out to get back to the caller.” 8 · Call Stack Task Answer Call Stack pane while paused inside calculate_item_total() Top to bottom: calculate_item_total , process_order , main Currently executing / who called it calculate_item_total / process_order Sequence of calls main → process_order → calculate_item_total Click the process_order frame: discount ? 8 (what you typed in section 1) Click the main frame: what can you inspect? order_code , prices , count , discount , flags — the locals of main Did selecting a frame execute any instructions? No So what does selecting a frame change? The context being inspected , not the current execution point The Call Stack pane is the stack of frames from CL04, made visible : each function that has been called but hasn't returned gets one frame with its own locals. The top frame is where execution actually is. Clicking a lower frame just changes which frame's variables the Variables pane and Debug Console show — the yellow current-line marker doesn't move and nothing runs. It's how you ask “what were the caller's values when it made this call?” See CL04 · Function Stack Frames . Say it aloud: “ main called process_order , which called calculate_item_total . Clicking a frame changes what I'm looking at, not what's running.” 9 · Find the bug The spec: total > $50 → mark as priority; total > $100 → also an extra $10 discount. The symptom: orders over $100 never get the extra discount. Task Answer from the key Why isn't the extra discount applied? The first if ( total > 50 ) is true for every value over 100, so execution enters that branch and skips the else if How would you fix it? Make the two conditions independent instead of mutually exclusive // The buggy shape: // The fix: if (total > 50) { if (total > 50) { /* mark priority */ /* mark priority */ } else if (total > 100) { // never } /* extra $10 discount */ if (total > 100) { // separate if } /* extra $10 discount */ } How to use the debugger to prove it (this is what “use the debugger to determine why” means): first remove or disable your old breakpoints (the handout says to), then put one on the first if , run with an order whose total is over 100, and Step Over one line at a time . You'll watch the arrow enter the first branch and then jump straight past the else if . The lesson: else if means “only if the previous condition was false,” and any number over 100 is also over 50. In general: if two conditions can be true at the same time and you want both effects, they can't be chained with else . (An equivalent fix is to test the stricter > 100 first — but then it must also mark priority, so separate if s are cleaner.) Say it aloud: “An order over $100 is also over $50, so the first branch wins and the else if never runs. I'd make them two independent if s.” 10 · Input redirection and launch.json Task Answer Update the executable after your fix gcc practice.c -o cece Create checkoff.in containing 10 echo 10 > checkoff.in Run with stdin from that file ./cece < checkoff.in \${fileDirname} when practice.c is open The absolute path of the directory containing the open file — e.g. /mnt/learncli/workdir/debugging-checkoff-practice \${fileBasenameNoExtension} practice Debug with stdin from checkoff.in — edit launch.json how? (blank in the key) Use the Debug with input redirected configuration and change the file after < to checkoff.in (details below) Breakpoint after the scanf ; value of discount discount = 10 The key leaves 10f blank — here is the full answer (from CL10 ). Debug active file launches your program directly, so the debugger has no way to feed it a file. Debug with input redirected instead launches Bash and lets Bash do the redirecting: "program": "/bin/bash", "args": [ "-lc", "\\"\${fileDirname}/\${fileBasenameNoExtension}\\" < \\"\${fileDirname}/checkoff.in\\"" ] After substitution that's effectively /mnt/.../practice < /mnt/.../checkoff.in . Only the path after < needs editing: checkoff.in must sit in the same folder as the open .c file (because it's built from \${fileDirname} ), or you write a longer path. Then pick that configuration from the debug dropdown — editing it doesn't help if you launch the other one. Two rebuild paths, don't mix them up. The terminal ./cece only sees changes after you re-run gcc (10a). The debugger, though, first runs preLaunchTask: build from tasks.json , which recompiles with -g every time you start it — so the debugger always uses your latest source, and you don't need a manual gcc for it. Say it aloud: “The redirected config runs the program through Bash so Bash can send checkoff.in to stdin; I just changed the filename after the < .”

title: Drill · Fresh Program, Same Skills
text: Drill · Fresh Program, Same Skills A new program with different names, values, and a different bug than the sample — so this tests the debugger skills, not memory of the walkthrough. Every value below was checked by actually compiling this program and running it under gdb . Best way to use it: copy the program into a file ship.c in your own environment and actually do each step in VS Code , then answer here. The answers are unspoiled until you get them right (or press Reveal). The program: ship.c — a shipment cost calculator Spec: cost = 2 dollars per pound + a handling fee typed by the user. A shipment over 50 lb is flagged heavy . A shipment over 100 lb also gets a $15 surcharge . The label should print in upper case. Run it with a fee of 5 unless a question says otherwise. 1 #include <stdio.h> 2 #include <ctype.h> 3 4 int sum_weights(int weights[], int n) { 5 int total = 0; 6 for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) { 7 total += weights[i]; 8 } 9 return total; 10 } 11 12 int process_shipment(char label[], int weights[], int n, int fee) { 13 for (int i = 0; label[i] != '\\0'; i++) { 14 label[i] = toupper(label[i]); 15 } 16 int weight = sum_weights(weights, n); 17 int heavy = 0; 18 int cost = weight * 2 + fee; 19 if (weight > 50) { 20 heavy = 1; 21 } 22 if (weight > 100) { 23 cost += 15; 24 } 25 printf("Weight: %d lb, heavy: %d\\n", weight, heavy); 26 return cost; 27 } 28 29 int main(void) { 30 char label[] = "pkg-b3"; 31 int weights[5] = {12, 31, 9, 46, 30}; 32 int count = 5; 33 int fee; 34 printf("Enter handling fee: "); 35 scanf("%d", &fee); 36 int cost = process_shipment(label, weights, count, fee); 37 printf("Shipment %s costs $%d\\n", label, cost); 38 return 0; 39 } Resist reading for the bug — in a checkoff you'd find it with the debugger . Section G below walks you through exactly that. A · Compile and run Fill in the blank Compile ship.c into an executable named steven . Check The name goes immediately after -o ; the source file can be before or after that pair. Fill in the blank Run it from the terminal. Check ./ is required — the current directory isn't on $PATH . Then type 5 at the prompt. Multiple choice You type 5 . The label starts as "pkg-b3" . What does the final line print for the label? pkg-b3 (unchanged) PKG-B3 Pkg-b3 Nothing — it crashes The toupper loop on lines 13–15 rewrites each character in place in the caller's array — the same idea as arrays being passed by pointer in CL04. True / False Typing steven (no ./ ) will run the program as long as you're in the same directory as the executable. True False False — the shell only searches the directories in $PATH , and . isn't one of them. That's why ./steven is needed. B · Regular breakpoint Set a breakpoint on line 7 ( total += weights[i]; ), start the debugger, and type 5 at the prompt. Fill in the blank At the first stop, what is i ? Check 0 — read it in the Variables pane. You're at the top of the first iteration. Fill in the blank What is weights[i] ? (Which pane or tab would you use to see it?) Check 12 . It's an expression, not a plain variable, so use the Watch pane or the Debug Console . Fill in the blank What is total at this first stop? Check 0 — it was initialised on line 5 and nothing has been added yet. Multiple choice Has the current weights[i] already been added to total ? Yes — that's why the line is highlighted No — the highlighted line is the one that's about to run It depends on the compiler You can't tell without stepping A breakpoint pauses before its line executes. total is still 0 while weights[i] is already 12: the += is queued, not done. Fill in the blank You press Continue . What is total at the next stop? Check 12 . Continue runs until the breakpoint is hit again — the same line, next iteration ( i = 1 ). The first weight (12) has now been added. True / False A breakpoint pauses execution after its line has executed. True False False — it pauses before . The current-line highlight always means “this is next,” never “this just ran.” C · Conditional breakpoint Keep the breakpoint on line 7 and restart. Now you only care about weights over 40. Fill in the blank What expression do you put in the breakpoint so it only stops when the current weight is greater than 40? Check Right-click the red dot → Edit Breakpoint… → Expression . It's a plain C expression (no if ). Fill in the blank Press Continue. What is i at the stop? Check i = 3 — the first weight over 40 is weights[3] = 46 . Fill in the blank And what is weights[i] at that stop? Check 46 . Fill in the blank What is total at this stop? (Hint: which items were skipped over?) Check 52 = 12 + 31 + 9. The debugger didn't pause for those three, but the program still ran them — a conditional breakpoint only changes when you stop, never what executes. True / False A conditional breakpoint stops the program from executing iterations where the condition is false. True False False. Those iterations still run normally — the debugger just doesn't pause for them. That's why total already includes 12 + 31 + 9. Multiple choice Which is a dangerous way to write the condition? weights[i] > 40 weights[i] >= 41 weights[i] = 46 weights[i] == 46 A single = is an assignment : it would overwrite weights[i] with 46 every time the line is reached — corrupting the program — and evaluates true every time. Use == to compare. D · Debug Console and Watch Stay paused at the stop from section C ( i = 3 , weights[i] = 46 ). Fill in the blank What do you type in the Debug Console to show the current value of total ? Check Just the variable name — the console evaluates it as an expression. It shows 52 . Fill in the blank Without executing the next line, what expression tells you what total will be after the current weight is added? Check You do the addition yourself in the console: total + weights[i] . Nothing in the program changes. Fill in the blank What number does that expression evaluate to? Check 98 = 52 + 46. Fill in the blank Type an expression that evaluates whether the current weight is greater than 40. Check A comparison yields true (C represents it as 1 ). Read-only — nothing changes. Multiple choice Which Debug Console entry would change the running program? total total + weights[i] total = 0 weights[i] > 40 Only the assignment changes state. Reading a variable or computing/comparing values just looks . This is exactly why the sample checkoff's answer to “did it change anything?” is no . True / False If you add total to the Watch pane, its value is refreshed each time execution pauses. True False True — Watch keeps an expression on screen and re-evaluates it at every stop, so you can step and watch it change without retyping it in the console. E · Step Over, Step Into, Step Out Remove the old breakpoint. Put one on line 16 ( int weight = sum_weights(weights, n); ) and restart. Multiple choice You want that call to run, but you don't want to follow it inside sum_weights . Which command? Step Into Step Over Step Out Continue Step Over runs the whole call in one jump. Fill in the blank After Step Over, what line number is highlighted? Check 17 ( int heavy = 0; ). Line 16 finished — weight now holds the function's result. Fill in the blank What value does weight hold now? Check 98 . Keep that number in mind for section G. Multiple choice Restart. This time you suspect the problem is inside sum_weights . Which command from line 16? Step Into Step Over Step Out Restart Step Into pauses on sum_weights 's first line (line 5), so you can step through it. Multiple choice You've watched two loop iterations and want the rest of sum_weights to finish, returning to its caller. Which command, and where do you land? Step Over — you land in main Continue — you land at the end of the program Step Out — you land back in process_shipment Step Into — you land in toupper Step Out finishes the current function and pauses in the function that called it: process_shipment . Multiple choice Right after that Step Out, has weight received the value returned by sum_weights ? Yes — the assignment is already complete Not yet — you're back on the call line with the assignment still pending; one more Step Over completes it No — the return value is discarded by Step Out It depends on the value of n Verified in gdb : after finishing, the value 98 is returned but weight still shows its old value until the rest of line 16 executes. (Exactly how VS Code highlights the line can vary a little, but the assignment is pending either way.) True / False On line 25's printf , Step Into will let you step through printf 's source code. True False False — there's no source for library functions, so Step Into behaves like Step Over. Only your own functions can be stepped into. Select all that apply Which are true of Step Out ? A. It finishes the rest of the current function B. It pauses back in the function that called the current one C. It runs the program to the end D. It deletes all breakpoints Check A and B. Continue is the one that runs until the next breakpoint or program end; Step Out only returns you to the caller. F · Call stack Restart and pause inside sum_weights (breakpoint on line 7). You typed 5 as the fee. Multiple choice Which lists the Call Stack pane top to bottom ? main , process_shipment , sum_weights process_shipment , sum_weights , main sum_weights , process_shipment , main sum_weights , main , process_shipment The top frame is the function executing now; each frame below it is the caller that's waiting. Reading the sequence from main gives you main → process_shipment → sum_weights . Fill in the blank Which function called sum_weights ? Check process_shipment — line 16. Fill in the blank Select the process_shipment frame without resuming. What is fee there? Check 5 — the value you typed, passed down from main as an argument. Multiple choice In that same frame, what does weight show? 98 — it's already been computed Not a meaningful value yet — line 16 hasn't finished, so it's uninitialised (often 0 or leftover junk) 128 — the correct sum The debugger refuses to show it The frame for process_shipment is paused mid-line-16, waiting for sum_weights to return. Its local weight hasn't been assigned yet. Select all that apply Select the main frame. Which variables can you inspect? A. label B. weights C. total D. count E. fee F. cost G. i H. n Check A, B, D, E, F — the locals of main ( cost isn't assigned yet). total , i , and n belong to other functions, so they aren't in main 's frame. True / False Clicking a different stack frame executes instructions. True False False — nothing runs. Multiple choice What does clicking a different frame actually change? The current execution point Which breakpoint is active The values stored in the variables Which frame's context you're inspecting Only the context you're looking at (Variables pane and Debug Console scope). The program's real execution point stays put in the top frame. G · Find the bug (with the debugger) Symptom: with a fee of 5, the program prints Weight: 98 lb, heavy: 1 and Shipment PKG-B3 costs $201 . The array's weights sum to more than 100, so the spec says there should be a $15 surcharge — but there isn't. Use the debugger; don't just stare at the code. Multiple choice Which is the best first debugger move? Rewrite the if on line 22 to use >= 98 Break just after line 16 and check the value of weight against the real sum of the array Keep pressing Continue until the program ends Change the surcharge from 15 to 20 Work backward from the symptom : the surcharge depends on weight , so first check whether weight is right. Changing the thresholds or the surcharge hides the bug instead of finding it. Fill in the blank What should weight be? (Sum the array by hand.) Check 12 + 31 + 9 + 46 + 30 = 128 . The debugger showed 98 — 30 short , which is exactly the last element. Multiple choice The array is correct, and the if on line 22 is correct for the spec, but weight is wrong. Where is the bug most likely? The array initialiser in main The printf on line 25 Inside sum_weights , which computes weight The toupper loop Only sum_weights produces weight , so that's where the wrong value is created. Step Into it from line 16. Fill in the blank Step Into sum_weights and step through the loop. What is the last value of i for which line 7 runs? Check 3. After that the loop exits, and weights[4] (30) is never added. Multiple choice Why does the loop stop after i = 3 when the array has 5 elements? The condition is i < n - 1 , i.e. i < 4 , so i = 4 is never processed — an off-by-one error n is passed in as 3 total overflows at 98 The debugger skips the last iteration n is 5 (you can confirm that in the Variables pane), so n - 1 is 4 and the loop only runs while i is 0–3. Fill in the blank Write the corrected loop condition. Check i < n — visit every index from 0 up to n − 1 . Fill in the blank After the fix and a recompile, what does the last line print for the cost with a fee of 5? (128 lb × 2 + fee + surcharge.) Check 128 × 2 + 5 + 15 = 276 . (Before the fix it was 98 × 2 + 5 = 201, with no surcharge.) Multiple choice The sample checkoff's bug had this shape. For x = 120 , which blocks run? if (x > 50) { /* A */ } else if (x > 100) { /* B */ } Only A Only B Both A and B Neither 120 > 50, so A runs and the else if is never even evaluated. Any value over 100 is also over 50, so B is unreachable — the fix is two separate if s. True / False A program that runs without crashing but prints a wrong answer can't be debugged with breakpoints — you can only find that kind of bug by adding printf s. True False False — wrong-answer bugs are exactly what the debugger is for: compare expected vs. actual at each step and find the first place they diverge (here, weight right after line 16). H · Input redirection, launch.json , and the terminal Fill in the blank Create a file checkoff.in containing the number 12 . Check > creates (or overwrites) the file with that content. Fill in the blank Run ./steven with stdin coming from checkoff.in . Check < redirects stdin . The prompt text still prints (it goes to stdout), but you don't type the fee. Fill in the blank Now add a second line, 7 , to the end of checkoff.in without erasing the first. Check >> appends. Using > here would erase the 12 . Multiple choice ship.c is the open file at /home/student/lab/ship.c . What is \${fileDirname} ? /home/student/lab /home/student/lab/ship.c ship lab The absolute path of the directory containing the open file. Fill in the blank For that same file, what is \${fileBasenameNoExtension} ? Check ship — the file name without its directory and without .c . Multiple choice You want the debugger to run ship with stdin from checkoff.in . Which debug configuration do you choose (and edit)? Debug active file Debug with input redirected Either — they're identical Neither — you must run gdb from the terminal Debug active file launches the executable directly, so nothing feeds it a file. Debug with input redirected launches Bash, which does the < redirection. Multiple choice Which args string in that configuration reads from checkoff.in in the same folder as the source file? "\\"\${fileDirname}/checkoff.in\\" < \\"\${fileDirname}/\${fileBasenameNoExtension}\\"" "\\"\${fileDirname}/\${fileBasenameNoExtension}\\" < \\"\${fileDirname}/checkoff.in\\"" "\\"\${fileDirname}/\${fileBasenameNoExtension}\\" > \\"\${fileDirname}/checkoff.in\\"" "checkoff.in" Program then < then the input file. Option C uses > , which would send output into checkoff.in and wipe it; option A is backwards. Multiple choice What does tasks.json do? Sets which breakpoints are active Defines tasks such as building/compiling (the build task that runs gcc -g before the debugger starts) Stores your program's input Lists the files in the project tasks.json = how the program is built ; launch.json = how it's run under the debugger. launch.json 's preLaunchTask is what wires the two together. Multiple choice Your program is stuck in an infinite loop in the terminal. What do you press? Ctrl + C — sends SIGINT , interrupting the running program Ctrl + D — sends end-of-file Ctrl + S Close the laptop Ctrl + C = interrupt ( SIGINT ). Multiple choice Your program reads with a getchar() loop from the keyboard until EOF . You've typed all the input. What do you press to say “no more input”? Ctrl + C Ctrl + D — signals end-of-file on stdin Enter twice Esc Ctrl + D = EOF for stdin. Ctrl + C would instead kill the program. Memorise the pair: C = Cancel/interrupt, D = Done/EOF.
