title: Explain It Aloud
text: Explain It Aloud A checkoff is oral : you'll be asked how can you tell? , why? , and what do you expect to happen? — often before you press anything. Practise answering out loud (or type your answer), then reveal the model answer. These are short on purpose: TAs want the right idea in a sentence or two, not an essay. 1. You're stopped on total += prices[i]; and total is 0 while prices[i] is 18. Has the 18 been added yet? How can you tell? Show model answer No. A breakpoint pauses before the highlighted line runs, so that line is about to execute, not finished. total still being 0 confirms it. 2. Why would you use a conditional breakpoint instead of a regular one? Show model answer When the line runs many times (like in a loop) but I only care about one situation. The condition is a C expression checked each time the line is reached; the debugger only pauses when it's true, but the other iterations still run normally. 3. How can you find out what a variable will be after the next statement, without running it? Show model answer Evaluate the arithmetic myself in the Debug Console — e.g. total + prices[i] . Evaluating an expression only reads values, so nothing in the running program changes. (An assignment like total = 0 would change it.) 4. In one sentence each: Step Over, Step Into, Step Out. Show model answer Step Over: run this line, including any function it calls, without entering the function. Step Into: if the line calls one of my functions, go inside and pause on its first line. Step Out: finish the current function and pause back in its caller. 5. What does the Call Stack show, and what happens when you click a lower frame? Show model answer It shows every function that has been called but hasn't returned yet, with the one executing now on top and main at the bottom. Clicking a lower frame runs nothing — it only changes which frame's variables I'm inspecting. The program's execution point stays where it was. 6. Talk me through how you'd find an unknown bug with the debugger. Show model answer A repeatable routine: 1. State expected vs. actual “It should have applied the surcharge; it didn't.” 2. Work backward from the symptom The surcharge depends on weight , so check weight first. 3. Breakpoint just before the suspect Not at the top of main — close to where the value goes wrong. 4. Predict, then step Say what you expect a line to do; Step Over or Into; compare. 5. Find the first divergence The first place actual ≠ expected is where the bug is (or feeds it). 6. Fix, save, recompile, re-run Then confirm the original symptom is gone. 7. What's the difference between launch.json and tasks.json ? Show model answer tasks.json defines how the program is built (the gcc -g ... command, using variables like \${file} ). launch.json defines how the debugger runs it (the executable path, gdb , program arguments, and a preLaunchTask that runs the build first). 8. Why does the “input redirected” configuration launch /bin/bash instead of the program itself? Show model answer The < redirection is a shell feature, not something the program understands. So the debugger starts Bash with -lc "program < file" ; Bash points stdin at the file, then runs the program under the debugger. To use a different input file I just edit the path after the < .

title: Common Mistakes on the Debugging Checkoff
text: Common Mistakes on the Debugging Checkoff Not obscure errors — the ones that look right. Read this tab right before your slot. 1. Showing up with the debugger not working. The handout says it in red: no extra time . Do the setup checklist on the first tab and make sure a test breakpoint really pauses — before your slot. 2. Reading the highlighted line as “already ran.” Breakpoints and every step stop before the highlighted line executes. Nearly every “is X already Y?” question in the sample depends on this. 3. Forgetting to restart the debugger between sections. The sample says “restart the program” several times. If you don't, you're still paused somewhere mid-run — your breakpoints won't hit where you expect, and your predictions will be about the wrong moment. Also remove or disable old breakpoints when told to (section 5 and section 9), or the program keeps stopping in places you no longer care about. 4. Typing = instead of == in a breakpoint condition or in the console. prices[i] = 40 doesn't test anything — it overwrites prices[i] with 40 and is always true. Comparisons use == , > , < . Assignments typed in the Debug Console change the running program, which is exactly what section 4d is asking about. 5. Using Step Into on a library call. There's no source for printf , scanf , or toupper , so Step Into just acts like Step Over. Step Into is for your own functions. 6. Editing the redirected configuration but launching the other one. If you pick Debug active file , nothing is redirected: the program sits there waiting for you to type the input (it looks frozen). Choose Debug with input redirected from the dropdown, and make sure the input file is in the same folder as the source (the path is built from \${fileDirname} ). Don't get < and > backwards either: > would erase your input file. 7. Not saving or recompiling after your fix. Save the file first. Then remember the two paths: the terminal runs whatever the last gcc produced (section 10a: re-run gcc to update it), while the debugger rebuilds with -g automatically via preLaunchTask . If the terminal still shows the old bug after you fixed it, you forgot to recompile. 8. Answering with the click, not the reason. You'll be asked “how can you tell?” and to predict before acting . Say the expectation first (“I expect to land on line 49 in process_order ”), then do it, then compare. A correct action with no explanation is worth less than one where you can say why. Related: the CL10 · Debugging lesson has the full launch.json / tasks.json reference and a worked bug hunt, and Checkoff 1 Prep covers the redirection commands ( < , > , >> ) this checkoff re-tests in section 10.

title: Lesson 2 · Compiling and Assembling
text: Lesson 2 · Compiling and Assembling Computers cannot understand Python, Java, or C. They understand machine code : binary instructions — strings of 1s and 0s — that tell the processor what operations to perform. Everything else is a translation layer built to spare humans from writing that. How we got from bits to C Era What you wrote What made it possible Before the 1950s Machine code , entered by switches, punch cards, or paper tape nothing — you were the translator Early 1950s Assembly language — human-readable mnemonics like add x8, x9, x10 Assemblers , programs that translate assembly into machine code Late 1950s High-level languages that abstract away the hardware and focus on logic and algorithms Compilers Machines still cannot read assembly — only machine code. The assembler exists precisely to automate that conversion, and it is what let programmers write and debug far more efficiently. The three languages the slides name Year Language Why it mattered 1957 FORTRAN (FORmula TRANslation) First widely adopted high-level language; built by IBM for scientific and engineering calculations 1958 LISP (LISt Processor) Pioneered functional programming and symbolic processing 1959 COBOL (COmmon Business-Oriented Language) Business applications; emphasized readability and portability; became the enterprise/financial standard Low-level vs high-level Machine code Assembly (low-level) C (high-level) Looks like 0b0000000010100100... add x8, x9, x10 return num * num; Readable by the machine humans, with effort humans, easily Tied to a specific processor yes yes no C is a compiled high-level language. To execute it, the program is first translated into assembly by a compiler , then the assembler translates that assembly into machine code . Two translations, two different tools. Interpreted languages like Python are executed differently — no separate compile-then-run step producing a machine-code file. Multiple choice What does a compiler translate, and into what? Assembly language into machine code A high-level language into assembly language Machine code into a high-level language Source code directly into output on the screen Compiler: high-level → assembly . Option 0 is the assembler . Two distinct programs, run one after the other — gcc just hides the seam by doing both. Multiple choice Why do assemblers exist? Because machines cannot read machine code Because C is faster than assembly Because machines cannot read assembly language — something has to convert it to machine code Because assembly is a high-level language Machines read only machine code. Assembly is for humans; the assembler automates the conversion. Option 0 has it exactly backwards.

title: Lesson 2 · Your First C Program
text: Lesson 2 · Your First C Program #include <stdio.h> int main () { printf ( "Hello, world!\\n" ); return 0 ; } Line Why it is there #include <stdio.h> printf is a standard library function. C does not automatically include any standard library functions — to use printf you must explicitly include stdio.h . int main() All C programs begin executing at main . It returns an int — the program's exit status . return 0; A successful execution returns 0 . An abnormal execution returns a non-zero value. Note the direction of that convention: 0 means success , which is the opposite of the usual "0 is false" intuition. Non-zero is how a program reports which thing went wrong. The C Standard Library A collection of pre-written functions for common tasks: input/output, string manipulation, mathematical operations, memory management. The functions are grouped into header files . A header file contains the declarations of the functions, macros, and types you can use. Term Meaning Function declaration the function's name, return type, and parameters Function definition the body of the function The header gives you the declaration so the compiler knows how to call the function; the definition lives in the compiled library. Header file Purpose Example functions <stdio.h> Input/output printf, getchar, putchar, fopen <stdlib.h> General utilities malloc, free, exit, atoi, rand <string.h> String manipulation strlen, strcpy, strcat, strcmp <math.h> Mathematical operations sqrt, pow, sin, cos, tan, exp <time.h> Date and time time, clock, localtime, gmtime Multiple choice You call strlen but forget #include <string.h> . Why is that a problem? The function does not exist without the include C automatically includes it anyway, so it is fine C does not automatically include standard library functions — without the header the compiler has no declaration for strlen Header files are optional in C The function's definition exists in the library either way, but the compiler needs the declaration from the header to know its return type and parameters. The slides state it plainly: "C does not automatically include any standard library functions." Multiple choice What does the value returned by main represent? The number of lines the program printed The program's exit status — 0 for success, non-zero for abnormal The amount of memory used Nothing; it is ignored The exit status . This is how the shell (and tools like make ) find out whether your program succeeded.

title: Lesson 2 · Compiling and Running with gcc
text: Lesson 2 · Compiling and Running with gcc Write your program. Save it with a .c extension — say hello.c . Open a terminal and cd to the directory where the program lives. Compile and assemble: gcc hello.c Run it: ./a.out gcc invokes the G NU C C ompiler. It converts your human-readable C code into a machine-readable executable file . Command Executable produced gcc hello.c a.out (the default) gcc hello.c -o hello hello gcc -o hello hello.c hello gcc hello.c -o hi hi The -o rule. The executable name must immediately follow -o . Everything else about the ordering is flexible — notice rows 2 and 3 produce the same result with -o hello on either side of the source file. What you cannot do is separate -o from its argument. Why ./ ? . means the current directory (straight from Lesson 1), so ./a.out says "run the a.out that is right here." The ./ is required because the current directory is not in your PATH — the list of directories the shell searches for commands. Type a bare a.out and the shell searches PATH , does not find it, and reports "command not found," even though the file is sitting right in front of you. This is a deliberate security decision: if . were on the PATH, dropping a malicious file named ls into a directory would hijack the real ls . If you named the executable hello , run it with ./hello . In-class problem — multiple select Which of these sets of commands compile, assemble, and execute the program in my_program.c ? Tick every one that works. A. gcc my_program.c then ./my_program.c B. gcc my_program.c -o my_program then ./a.out C. gcc my_program.c -o my_prog then ./my_prog D. gcc my_program.c then ./a.out E. gcc my_program.c -o my_program then ./my_program.c Check C and D. The single idea being tested: you run the executable, never the .c source file. A and E both try to execute my_program.c — that is source code, not a program. B renames the executable to my_program with -o , so a.out was never created; ./a.out fails. D uses the default name a.out and runs a.out . C names it my_prog and runs my_prog . Both are consistent.

B renames the executable to my_program with -o , so a.out was never created; ./a.out fails. D uses the default name a.out and runs a.out . C names it my_prog and runs my_prog . Both are consistent.

title: Lesson 2 · Variables and Types
text: Lesson 2 · Variables and Types Property Meaning Scope Where in a program you can use a variable Lifetime When the variable exists in memory Type The range of values the variable can represent, and how the value will be interpreted That second half of "type" is the one worth underlining. A type does not only bound the values — it decides what the bits mean . The same byte is 65 or 'A' depending on how you read it, which is the entire subject of the next tab. C numeric types Type Usual size Values stored Declaration char 1 byte integers char x; short 2 bytes signed integers short x; int 4 bytes signed integers int x; long 4 or 8 bytes signed integers long x; long long 8 bytes signed integers long long x; float 4 bytes signed real numbers float x; double 8 bytes signed real numbers double x; 8 bits = 1 byte. So an int is 32 bits, and a char is 8. "Usual" is doing real work in that table. The exact number of bytes for each C type might vary from one architecture to the next — which is why long is listed as "4 or 8." Never hard-code a size you did not measure. Measuring with sizeof The sizeof operator takes the name of a type and evaluates to the number of bytes used to store it. printf ( "number of bytes in an int: %lu\\n" , sizeof ( int )); printf ( "number of bytes in a short: %lu\\n" , sizeof ( short )); sizeof evaluates to an unsigned long , so print it with %lu — not %d . This is a real compiler warning you will hit. Multiple choice Which placeholder should you use to print sizeof(int) ? %d %s %lu %c sizeof evaluates to an unsigned long , so %lu . Multiple choice How many bits are in a typical int ? 4 32 8 64 4 bytes × 8 bits per byte = 32 bits . The "4" in the table is bytes, not bits — read that column carefully.

title: Lesson 2 · printf
text: Lesson 2 · printf C's printf is very similar to Java's System.out.printf : the caller supplies a format string to print. The format string contains formatting specifiers — special characters that print tabs ( \\t ) or newlines ( \\n ), and placeholders for values. A placeholder is % followed by a type-specifier letter , and for each placeholder, printf expects an additional argument . Placeholders Placeholder Used for Example Output %d Signed integer printf("%d", 25); 25 %u Unsigned integer printf("%u", 25); 25 %f Floating-point number printf("%f", 3.14); 3.14 %c Single character printf("%c", 'A'); A %s String printf("%s", "Hello"); Hello %lu Unsigned long (e.g. sizeof ) printf("%lu", sizeof(int)); 4 Special characters (escape sequences) A special character has a specific meaning or function in the language rather than simply representing ordinary text. In C, escape sequences use a backslash ( \\ ) to represent them — which lets you include characters that are difficult to type or represent directly. Sequence Name Meaning Example \\n Newline Moves to the next line "Hello\\nWorld" \\t Tab Inserts a horizontal tab "Name:\\tJohn" \\\\ Backslash Prints a \\ "C:\\\\Users" \\" Double quote Prints a " inside a string "He said \\"Hello\\"" \\0 Null character Marks the end of a C string "Hello\\0" %% Percent sign Prints a % when using printf printf("50%%"); Two different escape characters doing two different jobs. \\ introduces a special character; % introduces a placeholder. That is why a literal percent sign is %% and not \\% — it is escaping within printf's own notation, not C's. Match each specifier %d — choose — signed integer single character string newline tab a literal percent sign %c — choose — signed integer single character string newline tab a literal percent sign %s — choose — signed integer single character string newline tab a literal percent sign \\n — choose — signed integer single character string newline tab a literal percent sign \\t — choose — signed integer single character string newline tab a literal percent sign %% — choose — signed integer single character string newline tab a literal percent sign Check

title: Lesson 2 · Characters and ASCII
text: Lesson 2 · Characters and ASCII ASCII stands for American Standard Code for Information Interchange . It is a code that lets computers represent text using numbers. The C char type stores a numeric value — but it is most often used to hold the value of an ASCII character. Values worth memorizing Character ASCII value 'A' 65 'B' 66 'a' 97 '0' 48 space 32 '!' 33 Learn 65, 97, 48 and the rest follow: letters and digits run consecutively, and lowercase is exactly 32 above uppercase. With 8 bits An unsigned char holds the values [0, 2 8 −1] = [0, 255] . That is comfortably more than enough for the ASCII set. Bits are just bits. To give bits meaning you must assign them a representation , which defines how they correspond to meaningful information. Take the value 0b0100 0001 : • as a decimal integer it reads as 65 • as an ASCII character it reads as 'A' Nothing about the bits changed. Only the interpretation did. %c vs %d — the same value, two readings printf ( "%c\\n" , 'A' ); // A printf ( "%d\\n" , 'A' ); // 65 Give it a character and ask for a number: you get the ASCII code. printf ( "%c\\n" , 67 ); // C printf ( "%d\\n" , 87 ); // 87 Give it a number and ask for a character: you get the character with that ASCII encoding. The placeholder chooses the interpretation. The value being passed is a number either way. Character arithmetic Because a char is a number, you can do arithmetic with characters. printf ( "%d\\n" , 'a' - 'C' ); The ASCII value of 'C' is 67 and of 'a' is 97, so this prints 30 . The genuinely useful version of this trick is the constant 'a' - 'A' = 32 , the gap between lowercase and uppercase. Subtract it from a lowercase letter and you get the uppercase one — which is exactly how the in-class echo program works. Why we are learning this The slides make the point explicitly: ASCII is not specific to C. Computers ultimately represent all data using binary, including letters, digits, and symbols. Regardless of the language you use, characters must be represented numerically so the computer can store and process them. Learning ASCII is how you internalize the relationship between characters and their numeric representations — the same "bits are just bits" idea that runs through the entire course.

title: Bits Lab — one byte, three readings
text: Bits Lab — one byte, three readings Flip bits, or type a character, and watch the same 8 bits reported as binary, as a decimal integer, and as an ASCII character. type a character: or a number 0–255: 'A' = 65 'a' = 97 '0' = 48 space = 32 binary — printf("%d", c) — printf("%c", c) — Case-conversion check Set the lab to 'a' (97) and then to 'A' (65), and compare the binary. Only one bit differs. Multiple choice What is 'a' - 'A' ? 26 32 1 65 32 — 97 − 65. In binary that is the single bit worth 32 (the third from the left in a byte). Uppercase 0b0100 0001 vs lowercase 0b0110 0001 : one bit apart.

title: Lesson 2 · getchar , putchar , and EOF
text: Lesson 2 · getchar , putchar , and EOF Function What it does getchar() Reads one character from the input (a keyboard or a file) and returns it as an integer putchar(c) Takes the character stored in c and prints it to the output Both live in <stdio.h> , so you need that include. #include <stdio.h> int main () { int my_char = getchar (); printf ( "The user entered: %c\\n" , my_char); } EOF, and why getchar returns an int EOF stands for End of File . It is a special value returned by getchar() when there is no more input to read. EOF is the reason getchar() returns an int instead of a char . EOF must be distinguishable from any valid character. In the ASCII character set all valid characters are encoded as integers from 0 to 255 ; if EOF were encoded as a char it could collide with a real character value. The slides give the concrete case: if EOF were represented as 255 on a system where char is unsigned, it would conflict with the ASCII value for the ÿ character. An int is wider than a char , so there is room for a value outside 0–255 that no real character can ever equal. You signal EOF manually with Ctrl + D on Linux/macOS, or Ctrl + Z on Windows. The echo loop, two ways This reads characters until EOF and prints each one — it copies input to output, one character at a time. Explicit int main () { int c = getchar (); while (c != EOF) { putchar (c); c = getchar (); } } Concise (the idiom) int main () { int c; while ((c = getchar ()) != EOF) { putchar (c); } } The right-hand version reads inside the condition: first c gets the next character, then the while checks whether that character is EOF. The inner parentheses around (c = getchar()) are required — without them, precedence would compare getchar() to EOF first and assign the resulting 0 or 1 to c . Multiple choice Why does getchar() return an int rather than a char ? Because int is faster on modern hardware Because characters can be larger than one byte So EOF can be a value distinguishable from every valid character (0–255) Because putchar requires an int EOF has to be a value that no real character can equal . A char has no spare values left; an int does. True / False In while ((c = getchar()) != EOF) , the inner parentheses are optional style. True False They are required . != binds tighter than = , so c = getchar() != EOF would compare first and then assign the comparison result (0 or 1) into c — the loop would run, but c would never hold a character.

title: Lesson 3 · Arrays and #define
text: Lesson 3 · Arrays and #define Arrays in C are a fixed-size, contiguous block of memory holding elements of the same type. Unlike Java, a C array does not know its own size — there is no .length . The programmer must track the size separately, often with a #define d constant. Digit-counting program A classic example: read characters until EOF, and count how many times each digit '0'–'9' appears. #include <stdio.h> #define NUM_DIGITS 10 int main () { int ndigit[NUM_DIGITS] = { 0 }; int c; while ((c = getchar ()) != EOF) { if (c >= '0' && c <= '9' ) { ++ndigit[c - '0' ]; } } for ( int i = 0 ; i < NUM_DIGITS; i++) { printf ( "digit %d: %d\\n" , i, ndigit[i]); } } int ndigit[NUM_DIGITS] = {0}; declares an array of 10 ints and initializes every element to 0 (a partial brace initializer zero-fills the rest). Why ++ndigit[c - '0'] and not the tempting alternatives Expression What it actually does Verdict ++ndigit[c - '0']; c is a character code (e.g. '5' = 53). Subtracting '0' (48) converts it to the numeric digit value 5, a valid index 0–9. Correct ndigit[c]++; Uses the raw character code as the index . c for '5' is 53 — miles past the array's 10 slots. Wrong — out-of-bounds access ndigit['c'-'0']++; This is the literal letter 'c' (99) minus '0' (48) = a fixed constant, 51 . It never reads the loop variable at all. Wrong — nonsense fixed index, and still out of bounds The bug is easy to miss visually. ndigit[c] and ndigit['c'-'0'] both look like they involve the character we just read, but neither one does what ndigit[c - '0'] does: take the variable c 's ASCII code and subtract the code for '0' to land on a small index. Multiple choice Given char c = '7'; , what does c - '0' evaluate to? 7 55 48 A compiler error — you cannot subtract characters '7' is ASCII 55, '0' is ASCII 48. 55 − 48 = 7 — the numeric value of the digit character. This is exactly the trick used to convert a digit character to its value. True / False ndigit[c]++; is a safe, equivalent replacement for ++ndigit[c - '0']; when c holds a digit character. True False False. c is the raw ASCII code (e.g. 53 for '5' ), which is far larger than the array's 10 elements — an out-of-bounds write. #define : preprocessor text substitution #define NAME value is a preprocessor directive — a pure find-and-replace performed on the source text before compilation even starts . It is not a variable. #define NUM_DIGITS 10 const int num_digits = 10; Memory allocated None — it never exists at runtime Yes, a real memory location Type checking None — it is just swapped-in text Yes, it has a declared type When it happens Preprocessing, before compiling Compile time / runtime What the compiler sees Every occurrence of NUM_DIGITS literally replaced by 10 A named, typed variable Think of #define as your editor's "find and replace," run once, automatically, on the whole file before the compiler ever looks at it. No memory, no type, no runtime existence — it is gone by the time the compiler starts working. The four-stage build process Stage Tool Job 1. Preprocessor cpp Handles #include (pastes in header contents) and #define (text substitution). Produces expanded source text. 2. Compiler cc1 Translates the expanded C source into assembly language for the target processor. 3. Assembler as Translates assembly into object code (machine code) — a .o file. 4. Linker ld Combines your object file(s) with library object code (e.g. the implementation of printf ) into one final executable . gcc hello.c runs all four stages for you in one command, which is why nothing visibly "stops" between them. Multiple choice Which stage expands #define macros and #include directives? The compiler The preprocessor The assembler The linker The preprocessor runs first and handles all lines starting with # — pure text manipulation before any real compiling happens. Multiple choice Which stage combines your object file with the library code for functions like printf to produce the final executable? The preprocessor The compiler The assembler The linker The linker is the last stage — it stitches together every object file (yours and the standard library's) into one runnable program. C arrays vs Java arrays C array Java array Knows its own size? No — no .length Yes — arr.length Tracking size Programmer's responsibility (a separate size parameter, or a #define d constant) Built in to the array object Bounds checking None — out-of-bounds access is undefined behavior Runtime ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException If you write a C function that takes an array, you almost always need to pass its size too — the array itself carries no such information. Select all that apply Which statements about C arrays are true? A. A C array does not know its own length at runtime. B. Accessing an index past the end of a C array raises a runtime exception, just like Java. C. Programmers commonly use #define to name an array's size. D. ndigit[9] is out of bounds for int ndigit[NUM_DIGITS] when NUM_DIGITS is 10. Check A and C. C has no bounds checking (B is false — out-of-bounds access is undefined behavior, not a clean exception). D is false too: valid indices for a 10-element array are 0–9, so ndigit[9] is the last valid element, not out of bounds.

title: Lesson 3 · I/O Redirection
text: Lesson 3 · I/O Redirection Every running program has three standard streams, each identified by a small integer called a file descriptor : File descriptor Stream Default destination 0 stdin the keyboard 1 stdout the terminal 2 stderr the terminal stdout and stderr both print to the terminal by default, which is why you normally cannot tell them apart — until you redirect one of them. Redirection operators Syntax Effect cmd < input.txt Redirects stdin — the program reads from input.txt instead of the keyboard. cmd > output.txt Redirects stdout to output.txt , overwriting it if it exists. cmd >> output.txt Redirects stdout to output.txt , appending to the end instead of overwriting. cmd 2> errors.txt Redirects stderr only, to errors.txt . cmd > out.txt 2> err.txt Sends stdout and stderr to two separate files. > overwrites, >> appends. This is one of the most common mistakes in the course — running the same command twice with > destroys the first run's output. Demo programs readstdin.c #include <stdio.h> int main () { int c; while ((c = getchar ()) != EOF) { /* process c */ } } Reads from stdin (fd 0) via getchar() in a loop until EOF . writestdout.c #include <stdio.h> int main () { putchar ( 'x' ); } putchar() always writes to stdout (fd 1) — there is no way to redirect it to stderr by changing arguments. writestderr.c #include <stdio.h> int main () { fputc ( 'x' , stderr); /* or: fprintf(stderr, "x"); */ } Key point: putchar() can only ever write to stdout . To write to stderr , you must use a different function — fputc(ch, stderr) or fprintf(stderr, ...) — that takes the stream explicitly. Multiple choice You want a character written to stderr instead of stdout. Which function should you use? putchar(ch) printf("%c", ch) fputc(ch, stderr) There is no way to write to stderr in C putchar and plain printf are hard-wired to stdout . fputc(ch, stderr) (or fprintf(stderr, ...) ) explicitly names the stream. True / False cmd > output.txt appends to output.txt if the file already exists. True False False. A single > overwrites (truncates) the file. Use >> to append. Walkthrough: ./program < input.txt > output.txt 2> error.txt Suppose program reads numbers from stdin, prints valid results to stdout, and prints an error message to stderr for any invalid input line. Stream Where it goes stdin (fd 0) read from input.txt , not the keyboard stdout (fd 1) written to output.txt stderr (fd 2) written to error.txt What appears on the terminal nothing — both output streams were redirected to files Multiple choice Given ./program < input.txt > output.txt 2> error.txt , what shows up on the terminal while it runs? Only the error messages Nothing — both stdout and stderr were redirected to files Only the normal output Everything, because redirection doesn't affect the terminal Both 1 (stdout) and 2 (stderr) point at files here, so the terminal shows nothing from the program itself. Multiple choice Where do the program's error messages end up in that same command? output.txt the terminal error.txt input.txt 2> error.txt sends stderr specifically to error.txt , separate from stdout's output.txt .

title: Lesson 3 · Pipes
text: Lesson 3 · Pipes command1 | command2 connects command1's stdout directly to command2's stdin — no intermediate file is ever written to disk. The | character is called a pipe . Demo: producer and consumer producer.c #include <stdio.h> int main () { printf ( "apple\\n" ); printf ( "banana\\n" ); printf ( "cherry\\n" ); } Prints three lines to stdout, one fruit per line. consumer.c int main () { int c; while ((c = getchar ()) != EOF) { if (c== 'a' ||c== 'e' ||c== 'i' || c== 'o' ||c== 'u' ) putchar ( '-' ); else putchar (c); } } Reads stdin character by character and replaces each vowel with - . producer | consumer feeds producer's stdout straight into consumer's stdin: Input line (from producer) Output line (from consumer) apple -ppl- banana b-n-n- cherry ch-rry Match the input line to its piped output apple — choose — -ppl- b-n-n- ch-rry banana — choose — -ppl- b-n-n- ch-rry cherry — choose — -ppl- b-n-n- ch-rry Check Each vowel (a, e, i, o, u) becomes - ; every other character, including newlines, passes through unchanged. Chaining pipes Pipes chain: producer | consumer | wc -c feeds consumer's output into wc . Command Counts wc -c characters (bytes) wc -l lines wc -w words Multiple choice What does producer | consumer | wc -l print? The total number of characters printed by consumer The number of vowels replaced The number of lines consumer produced — 3, one per fruit Nothing; you cannot chain more than one pipe Pipes chain freely. wc -l counts lines of its stdin, which here is consumer's output — 3 lines, one per fruit. True / False A pipe connects one program's stdout directly to the next program's stdin, without writing an intermediate file. True False True. That's the whole point of | — no temp file, no disk I/O in between.

title: Lesson 3 · Strings
text: Lesson 3 · Strings C has no built-in string type. A C string is just a char array terminated by the null character '\\0' . Everything that works with strings ( printf("%s", ...) , strlen , ...) relies on finding that terminator. Literal initializers: quotes matter char str1[] = "hello" ; A double-quoted string literal automatically gets a '\\0' appended. str1 is 6 bytes: h e l l o \\0 . Valid C string. char str2[] = { 'h' , 'e' , 'l' , 'l' , 'o' }; A char-array initializer list does NOT add a terminator. str2 is only 5 bytes with no '\\0' — not a valid C string . Passing it to printf("%s",...) or strlen is undefined behavior. This is a real bug pattern, not a pedantic detail. {'h','e','l','l','o'} looks like it should behave like "hello" . It does not — there is no null terminator, so any function that scans for one will read past the end of the array into whatever memory happens to follow. strlen() vs sizeof() strlen(s) sizeof(s) What it measures characters up to (not including) the first '\\0' the array's total allocated byte capacity Needs <string.h> ? Yes No — it's a compile-time operator, not a function char str3[ 10 ] = "hi" ; printf ( "%lu\\n" , sizeof (str3)); // 10 — the array's declared capacity printf ( "%lu\\n" , strlen (str3)); // 2 — chars before the first '\\0' These two numbers can differ a lot, and mixing them up is a common bug (e.g. looping sizeof times over data that's really only strlen long). An early null terminator char str4[] = { 'h' , 'i' , '\\0' , 'X' , 'Y' , 'Z' , '\\0' }; printf ( "%lu\\n" , strlen (str4)); // 2 printf ( "%lu\\n" , sizeof (str4)); // 7 strlen stops at the first '\\0' it finds — giving 2 — even though the array physically holds 7 bytes and more data ("XYZ") sits after that first terminator. strlen has no way to know that data is there. Fill in the blank char a[] = {'h','i','\\0','X','Y','Z','\\0'}; — what does strlen(a) return? Check strlen stops counting at the first '\\0' , which is at index 2. It has no visibility into what comes after. Fill in the blank Same array — what does sizeof(a) return (its total byte capacity)? Check sizeof counts every element of the array, regardless of any '\\0' inside it — all 7 bytes. Multiple choice char bad[] = {'h','e','l','l','o'}; Why is this NOT a valid C string? It's missing the letter 'w' It has no terminating '\\0' , so functions that scan for the end of the string will read past the array C arrays can't be initialized with a list It should have used double quotes on each letter A char-array initializer list does not auto-append '\\0' the way a double-quoted string literal does. Without it, strlen / printf("%s",...) keep reading past the array's end — undefined behavior. String-handling functions like strlen , strcpy , strcat , and strcmp live in <string.h> — remember to include it.

title: RD02 · Arrays, Strings, I/O Redirection & Pipes — Self-Check
text: RD02 · Arrays, Strings, I/O Redirection & Pipes — Self-Check Covers the RD02 readings: Dive into Systems Appendix §Arrays & Strings, §I/O Redirection, §Pipes. Part 1: Strings & Arrays Q1 What makes strcpy dangerous compared to Java's string assignment? It runs slower than Java It performs no bounds checking — if the source isn't null-terminated, or is longer than the destination buffer, the result is undefined behavior (a buffer overflow) It requires <stdio.h> instead of <string.h> It only works on arrays of exactly 10 characters Java strings are immutable and bounds-checked by the runtime. C's strcpy just keeps copying bytes until it hits a '\\0' in the source — the programmer is responsible for making sure the destination is big enough and the source is properly terminated. Q2 In C, the programmer is responsible for ensuring a char array is properly null-terminated before treating it as a string. True False True. Unlike Java's safe, bounds-checked String , C gives you raw memory and trusts you to terminate it correctly. Q3 What does the C preprocessor do with a #define d constant? Allocates a memory location for it Type-checks every use of it Textually substitutes it wherever the name appears, before compilation Converts it into a function call Pure text substitution — no memory, no type. That happens entirely in the preprocessing stage. Q4 Given a valid digit character stored in char c , which expression correctly converts it to its numeric value? c - '0' c - 0 'c' - '0' c * '0' ASCII digit characters '0'-'9' are consecutive codes 48-57, so subtracting the code for '0' converts a digit character to its numeric value. Part 2: I/O Redirection Q1 Which operator redirects a program's stdin to come from a file? > >> < | < feeds a file's contents in as stdin. Q2 Difference between > and >> ? > is for stderr, >> is for stdout > overwrites the file, >> appends to it They are identical >> is only valid with pipes > overwrites; >> appends. Same stream (stdout by default), different file-open mode. Q3 Which file descriptor is stderr? 0 2 1 3 0 = stdin, 1 = stdout, 2 = stderr . Q4 cmd > out.txt 2> err.txt sends stdout and stderr to two separate files. True False True. Each redirection targets a different file descriptor, so they don't collide. Part 3: Pipes Q1 What does | connect? Two files on disk The left command's stdout to the right command's stdin The left command's stderr to the right command's stdout Two separate terminal windows A pipe is a direct stdout→stdin connection between two processes, with no file on disk. Q2 Pipes can be chained: a | b | c is valid and feeds a's output through b into c. True False True. Each | creates one connection; you can chain as many as you like. Q3 · Fill in the blank Which wc flag counts lines of input? Check wc -l counts lines; -w counts words, -c counts characters/bytes.

title: Lesson 4 · Function Stack Frames
text: Lesson 4 · Function Stack Frames Every time a function is called, the program allocates a chunk of memory for it on the call stack called a stack frame . That frame holds everything the function needs to run and to hand control back when it's done. What's inside a stack frame Field Purpose Return Address (RA) The address in the caller to resume execution at once the callee returns. Arguments The parameter values passed in by the caller. Local Variables Variables declared inside the function's own body. Caller — the function making the call. Callee — the function being called. Every call has exactly one of each. The stack pointer The stack pointer ( sp ) always points at the top of the stack — the edge of the most recently allocated frame. Event What happens to sp A function is called A new frame is pushed : sp moves to make room for it (grows the stack). A function returns The top frame is popped /deallocated: sp moves back, and that frame's memory is considered dead (conceptually "X-ed out" — its contents are no longer valid, even though the bytes may still physically sit in memory until overwritten). The stack grows with every call and shrinks with every return — a strict last-in-first-out order. The most recently called, not-yet-returned function's frame is always the one on top. Multiple choice What does a stack frame's Return Address (RA) store? The value the function will return The address in the caller to resume execution at once this function returns The address of the function's first local variable The size of the stack frame The RA is how the CPU knows where to go back to in the caller — not the function's own return value. Multiple choice When a function returns, what happens to its stack frame? It is popped/deallocated, and sp moves back down It stays on the stack forever It moves to the heap sp moves further up to make more room for it Returning pops the frame: sp moves back to where it was before the call, freeing that space for the next call. True / False The stack pointer sp always points at the bottom (oldest frame) of the stack. True False False. sp points at the top — the most recently pushed frame.

title: Lesson 4 · Call-Chain Walkthrough
text: Lesson 4 · Call-Chain Walkthrough Trace a chain of calls: main calls A , A calls B , B calls C . Watch the stack grow with each call, and unwind on each return. void C () { /* does work, returns */ } void B () { C (); } void A () { B (); } int main () { A (); } Step Call/Return Stack (top → bottom) 1 main starts main 2 main calls A A · main 3 A calls B B · A · main 4 B calls C C · B · A · main 5 C returns (frame popped) B · A · main 6 B returns (frame popped) A · main 7 A returns (frame popped) main 8 main returns (empty) Each call pushes a new frame on top; each return pops exactly one frame — the one on top, which is always the most recently called, not-yet-finished function. This is why the RA in each frame matters: when C returns, the CPU jumps to the RA stored in C 's frame, which points back into B . Multiple choice In the chain main → A → B → C , at the moment C is executing, how many stack frames exist? 1 2 4 0 One frame for each function still "in progress": main , A , B , and C itself — 4 total. Multiple choice When C returns, whose frame does the CPU resume executing in? B 's — the function that called C main 's A 's C 's own frame, restarted A return always goes back to the immediate caller — the RA stored in C 's own frame points into B , not further up the chain. True / False Stack frames are deallocated in the reverse order they were created (last pushed, first popped). True False True — the call stack is strictly LIFO (last-in, first-out).

title: Lesson 4 · Fixed-Size Integer Types
text: Lesson 4 · Fixed-Size Integer Types Plain int 's size can vary across compilers and architectures. <stdint.h> defines types whose byte width is guaranteed , which makes stack-frame byte-arithmetic (and this lecture's diagrams) predictable and portable. Type Bit width Byte width Typical use int8_t 8 bits 1 byte small counters, byte-sized flags, raw byte data int16_t 16 bits 2 bytes compact values with a known small range (e.g. audio samples) int32_t 32 bits 4 bytes general-purpose integers — matches a typical int int64_t 64 bits 8 bytes large counts, memory addresses/offsets, pointers-worth of data Why not just use int ? Because int 's size "might vary from one architecture to the next" — exactly the same caveat from Lesson 2's numeric-types table. In stack-frame diagrams we need to say precisely "this field is 4 bytes" and have that be true everywhere, so the lecture uses int32_t etc. instead of int / short / long . Multiple choice How many bytes does int32_t occupy, on every platform? 2 8 4 It varies by platform, same as int That's the entire point of <stdint.h> types — int32_t is always 4 bytes, unlike plain int . Fill in the blank Which stdint.h type is exactly 8 bytes wide? Check int64_t — 64 bits = 8 bytes.

title: Lesson 4 · Memory Diagram: add(int8_t a, int8_t b)
text: Lesson 4 · Memory Diagram: add(int8_t a, int8_t b) int8_t add ( int8_t a, int8_t b) { int8_t result = a + b; return result; } int8_t main () { int8_t x = add ( 3 , 4 ); } Build the callee's ( add 's) frame field by field: Field Size Value RA 8 bytes address back in main , right after the call to add a (arg) 1 byte 3 b (arg) 1 byte 4 result (local) 1 byte 7, once computed The sequence of events main calls add(3, 4) — a new frame for add is pushed , containing the RA and the argument copies a=3 , b=4 . add executes, computing result = 7 in its own frame. Just before add 's frame is deallocated, the return value 7 is written into an RV (return-value) slot that lives in the CALLER's ( main 's) frame . add 's frame is popped (X-ed out) — a , b , and result no longer exist. main resumes, reading the value from its own RV slot to initialize x = 7 . The return value does not live inside the callee's frame after the callee is gone — it is handed off into a slot in the caller's frame first. That's how the value survives the callee's frame being deallocated. Multiple choice Where does add 's return value end up living once add 's frame is deallocated? Nowhere — it's lost when the frame is popped It stays in add 's old frame, which is read later It was written into an RV slot in the caller's ( main 's) frame before add 's frame was popped On the heap The value is copied into the caller's RV slot before the callee's frame is deallocated — that hand-off is what lets main use the result afterward. Multiple choice What is the correct order of events for x = add(3,4) ? push add's frame → compute result → write result into caller's RV slot → pop add's frame → caller resumes using RV pop add's frame → push add's frame → compute result write RV slot → push add's frame → compute result → pop frame push add's frame → pop add's frame → compute result → write RV slot Frame pushed first, computation happens inside it, the result is written to the caller's RV slot while add's frame still exists , and only then is the frame popped.

title: Lesson 4 · Memory Diagram: Passing an Array
text: Lesson 4 · Memory Diagram: Passing an Array #define ARR_SIZE 5 int32_t example ( int32_t arr[ARR_SIZE], int32_t size, int32_t sum) { for ( int32_t i = 0 ; i < size; i++) { sum += arr[i]; arr[i]++; // mutates the CALLER's array! } size = 0 ; // does NOT affect the caller's size return sum; } The single most important idea in this lecture: Arrays are never copied into a callee's frame. Only an 8-byte pointer to the original array — which still lives in the caller's frame — is passed in. So in example 's frame, the field for arr is arr(8): pointer → caller's array — eight bytes holding an address , with a conceptual arrow pointing back up the stack into main 's frame where the real array data lives. Contrast with size and sum : as plain int32_t parameters, they are copied by value — the callee gets its own independent 4-byte copies. Changing size inside example ( size = 0; ) does not touch the caller's original size variable at all. But because arr is only a pointer back to the caller's actual array , a statement like arr[i]++; follows that pointer and does mutate the caller's original array data. The callee has no array of its own — every read and write through arr reaches straight into the caller's memory. Field in example 's frame Size Relationship to caller RA 8 bytes — arr 8 bytes a pointer back to the caller's actual array — not a copy size 4 bytes an independent copy of the caller's value sum 4 bytes an independent copy of the caller's value i (local) 4 bytes exists only inside example All pointers are 8 bytes on this architecture, regardless of what type they point to — a pointer to an int32_t array and a pointer to a single char are both 8 bytes, because a pointer just stores an address. Multiple choice When example(arr, size, sum) is called, what actually gets copied into the callee's frame for the arr parameter? A full copy of every element of the array Nothing — arrays cannot be passed to functions in C An 8-byte pointer to the original array, which still lives in the caller's frame Only the first element of the array Arrays are never copied into a callee's frame — only a pointer (8 bytes) back to the original data. True / False arr[i]++; inside example modifies the caller's original array. True False True. arr is a pointer to the caller's actual array data, so writing through it changes the caller's original. True / False size = 0; inside example changes the caller's original size variable. True False False. Plain int32_t parameters are copied by value — the callee's size is an independent copy. Select all that apply Which are true of passing int32_t arr[ARR_SIZE] as a parameter? A. The array's contents are duplicated into the callee's frame. B. Only a pointer (8 bytes) is passed. C. Changes to arr[i] inside the function are invisible to the caller. D. This happens even though the parameter is written as arr[ARR_SIZE] , with no explicit * . Check B and D. An array parameter decays to a pointer — only 8 bytes cross into the callee's frame, and mutations through it are visible to the caller (so C is false), even though the syntax never shows a * .

title: Lesson 4 · Pass-by-Value vs Pass-by-Pointer
text: Lesson 4 · Pass-by-Value vs Pass-by-Pointer Pass-by-value Pass-by-pointer What crosses into the callee's frame a copy of the value an address (a pointer) Callee modifies its parameter caller's original is unaffected caller's original is affected — the callee wrote through the address Typical C examples int32_t size , int32_t sum int32_t arr[ARR_SIZE] (array parameters decay to pointers), or an explicit int32_t *p This is exactly how arrays behave when passed to functions in C, even without an explicit * in the parameter list — int32_t arr[ARR_SIZE] decays to a pointer the moment it's used as a parameter. Plain scalar parameters ( int32_t , int8_t , ...) do not decay; they are copied. Match the parameter to its passing style int32_t size — choose — pass-by-value pass-by-pointer int32_t arr[ARR_SIZE] — choose — pass-by-value pass-by-pointer int32_t *p — choose — pass-by-value pass-by-pointer int8_t a (as in add(a,b) ) — choose — pass-by-value pass-by-pointer Check Any array parameter decays to a pointer; any explicit pointer parameter is pass-by-pointer; plain scalar types ( int32_t , int8_t , ...) are pass-by-value. Multiple choice A function takes int32_t x and does x = x * 2; inside. What happens to the caller's original variable? It doubles too It is unaffected — the callee only modified its own local copy It becomes garbage A compiler error occurs Plain scalar parameters are pass-by-value; the callee's x is a completely separate copy.

title: RD03 · Functions & Stack Frames — Self-Check
text: RD03 · Functions & Stack Frames — Self-Check Covers the RD03 reading: Dive into Systems Appendix §Functions. Q1 What triggers a new stack frame to be pushed? Declaring a global variable Calling a function Compiling the program Including a header file Each function call pushes a new frame; each return pops one. Q2 Which of these is stored in a function's own stack frame? The caller's local variables The next function it will call Its own local variables, its arguments, and the return address The entire program's source code RA, arguments, and locals — the three components covered in this lecture. Q3 Passing an array to a function in C passes a pointer, not a copy of the data. True False True. Only an 8-byte address crosses into the callee's frame; the array itself stays in the caller's frame. Q4 Modifying a plain int parameter inside a function changes the caller's original variable. True False False. Plain scalar parameters are copied (pass-by-value); the caller's original is untouched. Q5 Where does a function's return value get placed so the caller can use it after the callee's frame is gone? A return-value (RV) slot in the caller's own frame It stays in the callee's frame permanently A global variable The heap It's written into the caller's frame before the callee's frame is deallocated. Q6 Why does this lecture prefer int32_t over plain int in its diagrams? int32_t is faster int32_t has a guaranteed, portable size (exactly 4 bytes) everywhere, unlike plain int int cannot be used as a function parameter There is no real difference Predictable byte widths make the stack-frame arithmetic in the diagrams exact and portable. Q7 What does the stack pointer sp track? The number of functions defined in the program The address of main The return value of the current function The top of the call stack sp always points at the top of the stack — the most recently pushed frame. Q8 · Select all Which parameters would be pass-by-pointer in C? A. int32_t data[SIZE] B. int32_t count C. char *name D. int8_t flag Check A and C. An array parameter decays to a pointer, and char *name is an explicit pointer. B and D are plain scalars — pass-by-value. Q9 · Fill in the blank On this architecture, a pointer — regardless of what it points to — is always how many bytes? Check All pointers are 8 bytes: an address, not the data itself.

title: Lesson 5 · $PATH
text: Lesson 5 · $PATH The shell does not search the current working directory for executables. This is why ./hello requires the ./ even when hello is sitting right there — and it's a deliberate security decision, not an oversight. Why the shell won't search . Imagine your current directory is ~/Downloads , and it contains ~/Downloads/suspicious-stuff , which in turn happens to contain a malicious script named ls . If the shell searched the current directory first (or at all), simply running ls from inside suspicious-stuff could execute the fake ls instead of the real /bin/ls — silently, with no warning. Because . is never searched, that attack doesn't work: typing ls always searches $PATH and finds the real one. Running a program in the current directory always requires the explicit ./ . What $PATH actually is $PATH is a shell environment variable holding a colon-separated list of directories the shell does search for executables, in order, left to right, stopping at the first match . $ echo $PATH /home/student/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin Worked example Suppose PATH=/home/student/bin:/usr/bin , and both directories contain an executable named foo : Directory (search order) Has foo ? Used when you type foo ? 1. /home/student/bin yes Yes — first match wins 2. /usr/bin yes No — never reached Running foo executes /home/student/bin/foo , simply because that directory is listed first in $PATH . This is also how you can intentionally shadow a system command with your own version, by putting your own directory earlier in $PATH . Multiple choice Why doesn't the shell search the current directory for executables by default? It would be too slow Current-directory files can't be executable Security — it would let a maliciously named file (e.g. a fake ls ) in the current directory hijack a common command The current directory is always already in $PATH If . were searched, dropping a file named ls (or any common command) into a directory could silently run instead of the real program. Multiple choice PATH=/home/student/bin:/usr/bin , and both directories have an executable named foo . Which one runs when you type foo ? The one in /home/student/bin , because it's listed first The one in /usr/bin , because system directories take priority Both run, one after another Neither — ambiguous names cause an error The shell searches $PATH left to right and stops at the first match. True / False $PATH entries are separated by spaces. True False False — entries are separated by colons ( : ), not spaces.

title: Lesson 5 · Globbing
text: Lesson 5 · Globbing Globbing is filename expansion performed by the shell itself , before a command even runs. The shell looks at actual filenames in a directory and replaces the glob pattern with every name that matches it. Pattern Matches Example * any number of characters (including zero) *.c matches dog.c , a.c , .c ? exactly one character lab?.c matches lab0.c , lab1.c , not lab.c or lab10.c [abc] one character from the given set lab[01].c matches lab0.c or lab1.c only [a-z] one character in the given range [a-z]og.c matches dog.c , log.c Glob expansion happens before the command sees its arguments — by the time ls *.c runs, the shell has already replaced *.c with the literal list of matching filenames. Multiple choice What does ? match in a glob pattern? Zero or more characters Exactly one character One or more characters A literal question mark ? matches exactly one character — no more, no less. Select all that apply Given files lab0.c lab1.c lab10.c labX.c , which does the glob lab?.c match? A. lab0.c B. lab10.c C. labX.c D. lab.c Check A and C. ? matches exactly one character, so lab10.c (two extra characters) and lab.c (zero) don't match.

title: Lesson 5 · Regular Expressions
text: Lesson 5 · Regular Expressions A regular expression is a pattern-matching language used by a program (like grep ) to match against text content — not filenames. Character classes Pattern Meaning [abc] one character from the set [a-z] one character in the range [0-9] one digit Quantifiers Pattern Meaning * zero or more of the preceding character/group + one or more of the preceding character/group ? zero or one of the preceding character/group {n} exactly n {n,} n or more {n,m} between n and m , inclusive Anchors and escaping Pattern Meaning ^ start of line $ end of line \\. , \\* , etc. escape a special character to match it literally Match the regex piece to its meaning ^ — choose — start of line end of line zero or more one or more between n and m $ — choose — start of line end of line zero or more one or more between n and m * — choose — start of line end of line zero or more one or more between n and m + — choose — start of line end of line zero or more one or more between n and m {2,3} — choose — start of line end of line zero or more one or more between n and m Check Anchors ( ^ $ ) fix a position; quantifiers ( * + {n,m} ) control repetition of whatever came right before them. Multiple choice Who evaluates a regular expression? The shell, before the command runs A program (like grep ), against text content The filesystem The compiler Regex matching is done by the program reading the text — unlike globbing, which the shell does against filenames before the command even starts.

title: Lesson 5 · Globbing vs Regular Expressions
text: Lesson 5 · Globbing vs Regular Expressions Globbing Regular expressions What it is filename expansion text pattern matching Who performs it the shell a program (e.g. grep ) What it operates on filenames that exist in a directory the content/text of files or strings Example pattern *.c ^[a-z].*_[0-9]{2,3}$ Pattern language power simpler — * ? [abc] [a-z] more powerful — adds quantifiers ( + ? {n,m} ) and anchors ( ^ $ ) The classic confusion: * means something completely different in each context. In a glob , * means "any characters" all by itself — *.c matches any filename ending in .c . In a regex , * never stands alone conceptually — it means "zero or more of the character or group immediately before it." A bare * at the start of a regex, or after nothing meaningful, is either an error or matches literally nothing useful. To say "any characters" in regex you need .* (any single character, repeated zero or more times) — two symbols , not one. Multiple choice In a regular expression, what does a bare * quantify? Nothing — it means "any characters," same as in a glob The character or group that comes immediately before it The entire rest of the line Exactly one character Unlike glob's * , regex's * is a quantifier attached to whatever precedes it — it says "zero or more of that." Fill in the blank To match "any sequence of characters" in a regex (the equivalent of a glob's bare * ), you write which two-character sequence? Check .* — "any character" ( . ) repeated "zero or more times" ( * ). True / False find uses regular expressions for its -name patterns. True False False. find -name uses shell-style glob patterns, not regex — that's exactly why it's easy to confuse the two.

title: Lesson 5 · find
text: Lesson 5 · find find <where to search> -name <pattern> searches the filesystem recursively for files/directories by name. find can also filter by type, size, time, and permissions — but the core idea here is name matching. Crucially, find uses shell-style glob patterns, not regex. Basic examples Command What it finds find ./ -name dog.c searches recursively from the current directory; finds ./dog.c , ./src/dog.c , ./tests/dog.c — anywhere under . find ./src -name dog.c scoped to just src/ ; finds only ./src/dog.c Worked exercise set Given a directory tree under /home containing john and carla , where carla has comp211/labs/lab0.c , comp211/labs/lab1.c , and comp301/ , and john has psyc101/notes/lec1.note , lec2.note , lec3.note (no .c files anywhere under john ): Command Output find ./carla -name "*.c" ./carla/comp211/labs/lab0.c , ./carla/comp211/labs/lab1.c find . -name "comp*" ./carla/comp211 , ./carla/comp301 find ./john -name "*.c" no output — there are no .c files under john find ./carla -name "lab?.c" lab0.c and lab1.c — ? matches exactly one character, and both digits qualify find ./home/john -name "*.note" (run from / ) all three: lec1.note , lec2.note , lec3.note under john/psyc101/notes/ Note the second row: comp* matches both comp211 and comp301 — * just means "any characters," it does not care that the two names differ after "comp". Multiple choice find ./carla -name "lab?.c" against files lab0.c , lab1.c , lab10.c — what does it return? All three files lab0.c and lab1.c only Only lab10.c Nothing ? is exactly one character, so lab10.c (two extra chars) doesn't match — only lab0.c and lab1.c do. Multiple choice What kind of pattern does find -name expect? A regular expression A Python string method SQL LIKE syntax A shell-style glob pattern find uses glob patterns ( * ? [abc] ), the same language as filename expansion — not regex. Fill in the blank Write a find command that recursively searches from the current directory ( . ) for any file whose name ends in .c . Check find . -name "*.c" — . (or ./ ) as the search root, -name with a glob pattern. Single or double quotes around the pattern both work.

title: Lesson 5 · grep
text: Lesson 5 · grep grep <pattern> <file> searches a file's contents , line by line, for text matching a pattern, and prints the matching lines. Unlike find , grep uses regular expressions — a plain string is just a simple, valid regex. Basic and extended regex $ grep "ERROR" log.txt A literal string is itself a valid (simple) regex — this finds every line containing the text ERROR . $ grep -E "_[0-9]{2}$" users.txt The -E flag turns on extended regular expressions, which is required for {2} to work as a quantifier (in basic/default regex it would be treated literally). This finds usernames ending in exactly two digits preceded by an underscore — e.g. alice_01 . Piece-by-piece: grep -E "^[a-z].*_[0-9]{2,3}$" project/data/users.txt Piece Meaning ^ start of line [a-z] the line starts with a lowercase letter .* any characters in between (including other underscores) _ a literal underscore appears somewhere [0-9]{2,3} the line ends with 2 or 3 digits $ end of line So the whole pattern means: "a line that starts with a lowercase letter, contains an underscore somewhere, and ends with 2 or 3 digits." A username like steven_302 matches; Steven_302 (capital S) does not. Multiple choice What does a plain string like "ERROR" mean as a grep pattern? It's invalid — grep requires special regex syntax A simple, valid regex that matches the literal text "ERROR" anywhere on the line It matches only lines that are exactly "ERROR" and nothing else It's treated as a glob pattern A plain string is itself a valid (trivial) regular expression — it matches that literal text anywhere in the line. Multiple choice Why is -E needed for grep -E "_[0-9]{2}$" to work as intended? -E makes grep case-insensitive -E is required before any regex will work at all -E enables extended regex, so {2} is treated as a quantifier instead of literal text -E searches multiple files Without -E , basic regex treats {2} as literal characters, not a repeat-count quantifier. True / False grep uses shell-style glob patterns, the same as find . True False False. grep uses regular expressions ; find -name uses globs . Mixing these up is the most common error in this unit. Fill in the blank Write a grep (extended, -E ) command that prints lines from users.txt starting with a lowercase letter and ending in exactly 2 or 3 digits. Check Something like grep -E "^[a-z].*[0-9]{2,3}$" users.txt — anchors at both ends, [a-z] for the first character, and [0-9]{2,3} for 2–3 trailing digits.

title: Checkoff 1 · What to Expect
text: Checkoff 1 · What to Expect This is not lecture content — it is drill material built from a released sample checkoff (a blank version and its solution). The real checkoff mirrors this sample's style and topic coverage , but with different specifics: different filenames, a different repo, a different order. The goal here is command fluency — knowing which command/flag/operator solves a given spec on sight — not memorizing this exact sequence of 24 tasks. Format What that means Practical, oral, one-on-one You sit with a TA and perform tasks live in a terminal while they watch and ask you to explain what you're doing. Time Averages about 15 minutes ; you're given a 30-minute slot . Setup is on you You must have your container set up beforehand . No extra time is given if it isn't — that time comes out of your slot. Redo policy You can retake it during office hours the following week , but a redo caps out at a maximum score of 80/100 . The practical format changes what "studying" means. A quiz rewards recognizing the right answer among choices; a checkoff rewards typing the right command from a spoken/written spec, under a TA's eyes, with no menu of options in front of you. That is exactly why the Drill tab below leans heavily on fill-in-the-blank questions where you type the actual command — that's the closest this guide can get to checkoff conditions.

title: Walkthrough · Worked Through the Sample Checkoff's 24 Tasks
text: Walkthrough · Worked Through the Sample Checkoff's 24 Tasks Each group below is a cluster of tasks from the released sample that test the same underlying idea . Read the task, then the command, then why that command/flag/operator is the one that's correct — that reasoning is what transfers to a checkoff with different specifics. 1–3 · Getting oriented and cloning Task Command 1. Confirm you're in /mnt/learncli/workdir pwd 2. Clone the checkoff repo git clone https://github.com/COMP211-McMahon/cli-checkoff-practice.git 3. Move into the cloned directory cd cli-checkoff-practice pwd (print working directory) is the reflex you should have before doing anything else in a checkoff — it costs one second and prevents you from running every subsequent command from the wrong place. git clone <url> downloads the repo into a new directory named after the repo itself (here, cli-checkoff-practice ) — you don't create that directory yourself, git clone does. Then cd into it like any other directory. 4–5 · Creating a file vs. appending to it Task Command 4. Create student.txt containing exactly CLI practical ready echo "CLI practical ready" > student.txt 5. Append your name to the end of the file echo "[Your name]" >> student.txt > overwrites/creates; >> appends. Task 4 uses > because the file doesn't exist yet (or you're fine replacing it). Task 5 must use >> — using > here would silently destroy the line from task 4 and replace the file with just your name. This single character is the most common way students lose data on a checkoff without any error message telling them so. 6 · Compiling with -o Task Command Compile io_demo.c as io_demo gcc io_demo.c -o io_demo Compile classify.c as classify gcc -o classify classify.c Both compile successfully — the two examples are deliberately written in opposite orders to make the point: -o <name> can appear before or after the source file, but the executable name must immediately follow -o . Forgetting -o entirely leaves you with the default name a.out , which still runs fine but doesn't satisfy a task that names a specific executable. 7a–7c · The three redirection operators Task Command 7a. stdin from sample_input.txt , stdout to terminal ./io_demo < sample_input.txt 7b. stdin typed interactively, stdout to output.txt ./io_demo > output.txt (or 1> output.txt ), then type lines, then Ctrl+D (macOS/Linux) or Ctrl+Z (Windows) for EOF 7c. stdin from numbers.txt , stdout to positive.txt , stderr to errors.txt ./classify < numbers.txt > positive.txt 2> errors.txt Three streams, three operators, and they compose: < redirects stdin (fd 0), > redirects stdout (fd 1), 2> redirects stderr (fd 2). The order of the redirections after the command doesn't matter — ./classify > positive.txt < numbers.txt 2> errors.txt works identically. What matters is that each stream gets its own operator : you cannot combine stdout and stderr into one > . Note also there is no space between the file-descriptor number and the operator — it's 2> , not 2 > (a space there is a syntax error). 8–9 · Viewing output and command history Task Command 8. Display output.txt , positive.txt , errors.txt cat output.txt , cat positive.txt , cat errors.txt 9. Re-run the previous command without retyping it press ↑ (Up arrow) , then Enter The shell keeps a command history you can walk back through with the Up/Down arrows — this is worth demonstrating explicitly if a TA asks you to "run that again," since retyping a long command is slower and more error-prone than recalling it. 10–12 · Combining pipes and redirects Task Command 10. Read sample_input.txt into io_demo , its stdout to piped_output.txt , then display it cat sample_input.txt | ./io_demo > piped_output.txt , then cat piped_output.txt 11. Read sample_input.txt → io_demo → a line-counting command → terminal cat sample_input.txt | ./io_demo | wc -l 12. numbers.txt → io_demo → classify → terminal ./io_demo < numbers.txt | ./classify A pipe ( | ) connects one running program's stdout directly to another running program's stdin — no intermediate file. Task 11 shows pipes chain : as many | as there are hand-offs between programs ( wc -l counts lines). Task 12 is the one students most often get wrong. The instinct is "three things are connected, so use two pipes" — but numbers.txt is a file , not a running program, so it cannot sit on the left of a pipe. The first hop must be a redirect ( < ) because a file is feeding a program; the second hop is a pipe ( | ) because one running program is feeding another. Mixing operator types on purpose, based on what's actually on each side, is the skill being tested. 13–16 · Building a directory tree, then verifying it Task 13 asks for this structure, built with directory/file-creation commands only (no text editor): cli_lab/ ├── docs/ │ ├── notes.txt │ └── drafts/ │ └── outline.txt ├── data/ │ ├── raw/ │ │ └── input.csv │ └── processed/ └── archive/ └── old.txt Task Command 13. Build the tree (dirs, then files) mkdir -p cli_lab/docs/drafts cli_lab/data/raw cli_lab/data/processed cli_lab/archive touch cli_lab/docs/notes.txt cli_lab/docs/drafts/outline.txt cli_lab/data/raw/input.csv cli_lab/archive/old.txt 14. Return to the checkoff dir with an absolute path cd /mnt/learncli/workdir/cli-checkoff-practice 15. Verify the tree structure tree cli_lab 16. Clear the screen clear mkdir -p creates every missing directory in a nested path in one shot — without -p , mkdir cli_lab/docs/drafts would fail unless cli_lab/docs already existed. It also doesn't error if a directory already exists, which makes it safe to re-run. touch creates any number of empty files in a single call — no editor needed, which is exactly what the task requires. tree is the command that visually confirms a directory structure at a glance, which is why it's the answer to "which command verifies this." 17–19 · Hidden files Task Command 17. Display contents of cli_lab/docs ls cli_lab/docs 18. Create a hidden empty file .review in cli_lab/docs touch cli_lab/docs/.review 19. Re-run step 17 — is .review visible? No with plain ls ; visible with ls -a cli_lab/docs A filename starting with . is hidden by convention , and plain ls omits it. It isn't invisible or special-cased by the filesystem — it's just that ls 's default behavior skips anything starting with a dot. -a ("all") tells ls to include hidden entries, plus the always-present . (current dir) and .. (parent dir) entries. 20–23 · Relative vs. absolute paths in cp / mv Task Command 20. cd into cli_lab/data/processed cd cli_lab/data/processed 21. From there, copy cli_lab/docs/notes.txt into the current dir, both paths relative cp ../../docs/notes.txt . 22. Move cli_lab/archive/old.txt into cli_lab/data/raw/ , both paths absolute mv /mnt/learncli/workdir/cli-checkoff-practice/cli_lab/archive/old.txt /mnt/learncli/workdir/cli-checkoff-practice/cli_lab/data/raw/ 23. Copy all of cli_lab/docs to a new cli_lab/docs_backup cp -r cli_lab/docs cli_lab/docs_backup From cli_lab/data/processed , ../../ walks up two levels back to cli_lab , then docs/notes.txt reaches the file — .. means "parent directory," stacked once per level. The destination . means "the current directory, keep the same filename." Task 22 does the identical move with absolute paths instead — slower to type, but unambiguous regardless of where you currently are. Task 23 needs -r (recursive) because cp on a bare directory errors out by default — a directory isn't a single file cp knows how to copy without being told to descend into it and copy everything inside, recursively. 24 · Cleaning up — rm -rf Task Command Remove the checkoff directory and everything in it cd .. then rm -rf cli-checkoff-practice -r (recursive) is required to remove a directory and its contents; -f (force) suppresses the "are you sure?" prompts for every file inside. Together, rm -rf is irreversible — there is no trash can, no undo. You must cd .. out of the directory first (you can't remove your current working directory out from under yourself), and you should always double-check pwd /the path before pressing enter — especially that you are not accidentally one level up or down from where you think you are.
