title: Mastery: CL04 · Function stack frames & memory diagrams (+ RD03)
text: What a call does to memory, how to draw it the way the course expects, what is copied versus shared, and what the reading adds about functions, prototypes and pass-by-value. The stack manages function calls. Each call gets a stack frame (an activation record) holding the return address (RA) , the arguments and the local variables . Caller makes the call; callee is the function called. The stack pointer (sp) marks the current top of the stack. In the course’s diagrams the stack grows downward, toward lower addresses : a new frame is drawn below the caller’s, and sp moves down with it. On return, the callee places its return value in the caller’s frame (labelled RV(callee) ), its frame is deallocated (put an X through it) and sp moves back up . The old bytes may still be there physically, but the memory is no longer valid and gets reused by the next call. Draw sizes in bytes: RA (8) , an int8_t is 1, int32_t 4, a pointer 8. main ’s RA is just “return to the OS” (shown as 0). Return addresses are line numbers in the diagrams. Pass by value: scalar arguments are copies ; changing them never changes the caller. Arrays are not copied: the callee gets an 8-byte pointer ( pointer to stack , drawn with an arrow) to the caller’s array, so element changes are visible. #define names are replaced by the preprocessor, so they take no space in any frame. Functions must be declared before use : put a prototype (name, return type, parameters) above main . Common trap: Drawing a callee’s frame above the caller, or letting a deallocated frame stay un-X’d. Common trap: Forgetting the RV(...) slot: the return value goes in the caller’s frame, not the callee’s. Common trap: Copying a whole array into the callee’s frame. Only an 8-byte pointer goes in. Common trap: Giving a #define constant its own box in the diagram. Common trap: Thinking local variables survive the call: they die with their frame, which is why returning a pointer to a local is a bug and why unbounded recursion overflows the stack.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What is the stack and what is a stack frame? — The stack is the area of memory managing function calls. A stack frame is one function’s workspace: return address, arguments and local variables.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Caller vs callee? — The caller makes the call; the callee is the function being called. Every call has one of each.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What is the stack pointer (sp)? — It holds the address of the current top of the stack. It moves to make room on a call and moves back on a return.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Which direction does the stack grow in the course diagrams? — Toward lower addresses: a new frame is drawn below the caller’s frame.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What does the return address (RA) record? — Where in the caller execution continues after the callee returns. ( main ’s RA is the OS, drawn as 0.)

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Where does the return value go and how is it labelled? — Into the caller’s frame, labelled RV(callee) .

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What do you do to the diagram when a function returns? — Put an X through its frame and move sp back up. Its data may remain but is invalid and will be reused.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Why do local variables disappear when a function returns? — They live in the callee’s frame, which is deallocated on return.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: How is an array parameter represented in a frame? — As an 8-byte pointer to stack with an arrow to the original array in the caller’s frame. Nothing is copied.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Pass by value vs pass by pointer? — By value: the callee gets a copy, so changes are invisible to the caller. By pointer: the callee gets an address and can change the original.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Sizes to draw: RA, int8_t, int16_t, int32_t, int64_t, pointer? — 8, 1, 2, 4, 8, 8 bytes.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Does #define SIZE 5 get a box in a stack frame? — No. The preprocessor replaces it with 5 in the code, so it is not stored in any frame.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What is a function prototype and why put it above main? — It declares a function’s name, return type and parameter list so it can be called before its full definition appears.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Why must functions be declared before they are called? — The compiler must know a function’s type information (return type and parameters) before the call.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What goes wrong with deep or endless recursion? — Each call pushes another frame; the stack runs out of space (a stack overflow).

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What is a process? — A running instance of a program (active), with its own memory, CPU state and resources. A program on its own is passive code.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Main calls foo . In the course’s memory diagrams, where is foo’s frame drawn and which way does the stack grow? — New frames are drawn below the caller and sp moves down.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What happens to the stack pointer when a new function’s frame is created? — sp always points at the top (the newest frame).

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What does the return address (RA) in a frame represent? — The CPU needs it to resume the caller at the right line.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Main calls add , which returns a value main needs. What label marks that location in main’s frame? — The return value is placed in the caller’s frame as RV(callee) .

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Why do we put an X through a stack frame after its function returns? — Deallocated means invalid, not zeroed.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Using the course sizes (RA is 8 bytes), how many bytes does each frame take? int8_t add(int8_t a, int8_t b) { int8_t result = a + b; return result; } /* main: */ int8_t x = 5, y = -10; int8_t result = 2 * add(x, y); // main also holds RV(add) (1 byte) — add: RA 8 + a 1 + b 1 + result 1 = 11. main: RA 8 + x 1 + y 1 + result 1 + RV(add) 1 = 12.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Fill in each variable as the program runs. void C(int z) { int c = z + 1; } void B(int y) { int b = y * 2; C(b); } void A() { int a = 10; B(a); } int main() { A(); } — a (10) is copied into y; b = 20 is copied into z; c = z + 1 = 21. At C’s deepest point four frames exist: main, A, B, C.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames

( square returns before addOne is called.) int square(int x) { int result = x * x; return result; } int addOne(int x) { int result = x + 1; return result; } int calculate() { int answer = addOne(square(5)); return answer; } — The inner call finishes first: square(5) = 25 is placed in RV(square), its frame is X’d, and only then is addOne(25) called. addOne’s frame may reuse the memory square’s frame used.

The callee’s sum is a copy (it reaches 15 and is discarded), so main’s sum stays 7. It returns arr[0], which is now 2.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Fill in the byte sizes shown in the diagram of this function’s frame (course sizes). int32_t example(int32_t arr[], int32_t size) { int16_t i; } /* frame: */ RA (8) arr (__0__): pointer to stack size (__1__) i (__2__) — An array parameter is a pointer (8 bytes). int32_t is 4 bytes. int16_t is 2 bytes.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: In calculate , square(5) returns, and then addOne is called. Where can addOne’s frame be placed? — After square returns, sp moves back, so the next call can occupy that same memory.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Given void f(int32_t a, int32_t b[], int32_t *c, char s[]) , select all parameters drawn as an 8-byte “pointer to stack” in f’s frame. — Array parameters decay to pointers and explicit pointers are pointers; a plain scalar is copied by value.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Fill in main’s values. (An int8_t holds −128 to 127 and wraps when stored.) int8_t scale(int8_t v[], int32_t n, int8_t k) { for (int32_t i = 0; i < n; i++) { v[i] = v[i] * k; } k = 0; return v[0]; } /* main: */ int8_t d[3] = {60, 2, 3}; int8_t r = scale(d, 3, 3); — 60 × 3 = 180, which wraps when stored into an int8_t: 180 − 256 = −76. The array is shared so main sees it; r is the returned (wrapped) value; the callee’s k = 0 was only a copy.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Fill in the results. void inc(int *p) { (*p)++; } void twice(int *p) { inc(p); inc(p); } /* main: */ int k = 5; twice(&k); — Both frames get the address of main’s k, so each inc writes into main’s frame: 5 → 6 → 7. At the deepest point the stack holds main, twice and inc.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Fill in the results for this program. void E() { int e = 50; } void D() { int d = 40; E(); } void C() { int c = 30; } void B() { int b = 20; C(); } void A() { int a = 10; B(); D(); } int main() { A(); } — The deepest chains are main → A → B → C and main → A → D → E: four frames. By the time main returns, A and everything below it have returned and been X’d, leaving only main.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Which statement about #define SIZE 5 and int values[SIZE]; in main is correct? — After preprocessing the code reads int values[5]; .

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Describe, as you would draw it on paper, the memory diagram just after twice_all returns. Include every frame (with fields, byte sizes and values), the arrow, the RV slot, any X’d frame and where sp is. #define N 3 int32_t twice_all(int32_t v[N], int32_t k) { for (int32_t i = 0; i < N; i++) { v[i] = v[i] * k; } k = 0; return v[N - 1]; } int main(void) { int32_t nums[N] = {1, 2, 3}; int32_t k = 4; int32_t last = twice_all(nums, k); } — Only main ’s frame is live, with sp at its edge: RA (8): 0 , nums (12): [4, 8, 12] , k (4): 4 , last (4): 12 , and the leftover RV(twice_all) (4): 12 . twice_all’s frame below it is X’d out (its RA, v (8): pointer to stack , k (4) crossed 4 → 0, and i (4) would show 3). There is no box for N: it was replaced by 3 by the preprocessor. nums changed because v pointed at it; main’s k is still 4 because the callee’s k was a copy.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Write a prototype and a full definition for int max3(int a, int b, int c) that returns the largest of three ints, using a documentation comment in the style the reading recommends. Then explain where the prototype goes and why. — int max3(int a, int b, int c); // prototype, above main /* max3: finds the largest of three integers * a, b, c: the values to compare * returns: the largest of a, b and c */ int max3(int a, int b, int c) { int best = a; if (b > best) best = b; if (c > best) best = c; return best; } The prototype goes above main (or the whole definition does) because C needs a function’s return type and parameters before it is called. Parameters are copies, so changing best or a never affects the caller.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Teach it. Walk through everything that happens in memory when main calls add(x, y) and gets a value back: frames, arguments, return address, return value, sp, and what happens afterwards. — Call pushes a frame (RA, args, locals). The callee works, stores the result in RV(add) in main’s frame, and returns: its frame is X’d and sp moves back, so main can continue at the saved return address.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Explain how the stack explains two classic problems: returning a pointer to a local variable, and an infinite recursion crashing the program. — The stack only holds data for functions that are still active. Dead frames are reclaimed, so pointers into them dangle; and the stack is finite, so unbounded calls exhaust it.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: You know Java. Explain how functions in C differ from methods, what “passed by value” means, and why prototypes matter. — A C function is a free-standing unit with a typed signature. Its parameters are copies living in its own frame; the compiler needs a prototype before the call to check types.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: In the course’s memory diagrams, which way does the stack grow as functions are called? — Each call places a new frame below the caller’s, and sp moves down.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What does the stack pointer (sp) represent? — sp moves down when a frame is created and back up when it is removed.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: A function returns. What happens to the stack pointer? — The callee’s frame is deallocated, so sp returns to the top of the caller’s frame.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What does a frame’s return address (RA) tell the program? — It is a location in the caller’s code.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: A diagram entry reads count (2): 7 . What does the 2 represent? — The number in parentheses is the size in bytes (an int16_t).

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Main calls a function named scale that returns a value main needs. Which label marks that slot in main’s frame? — RV stands for return value, labelled with the callee’s name.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: When a function returns, which of these should you do in the diagram? Select all that apply. — The frame is deallocated and sp moves back; the old bytes are simply invalid.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Which of these may be stored in a function’s stack frame? Select all that apply. — Locals, parameters and the return address.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: The active frames are, from higher to lower addresses: main , mid , leaf . leaf is executing and then returns to mid . What do the active frames look like now? — Only the returning function’s frame is removed.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: int inner(int n) { return n + 1; } int outer(int x) { int y = inner(x); return y * 2; } int main() { int r = outer(4); return 0; } While inner is executing, what is the order of active frames from highest to lowest address? — Each call is pushed below its caller, so the nesting order is main, outer, inner.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Put these events in order for the program below. int inc(int n) { int r = n + 1; return r; } int main() { int y = inc(9); } Two events are impossible. — Frame, argument, local, return value into the caller’s RV slot, deallocate, sp back, then the caller finishes its assignment.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Put these events in order for this nested call. Two events are impossible. int sq(int a) { int s = a * a; return s; } int twice_sq(int b) { int t = sq(b); return t * 2; } int main() { int z = twice_sq(3); } — Calls nest: sq runs and returns entirely inside twice_sq, whose own frame is deallocated afterwards, before main assigns z.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What does it mean to pass an argument by value ? — Changing the parameter changes only the copy.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: void set(int32_t v) { v = 99; } int main() { int32_t v = 5; set(v); } What is main’s v after set returns? — The parameter is a copy in set’s frame.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: void fill(int32_t arr[]) { arr[0] = 7; } int main() { int32_t a[3] = {1, 2, 3}; fill(a); } What is a[0] after fill returns? — arr is a pointer to the caller’s array, so the write is visible.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Fill in main’s values after the call. void change(int32_t k, int32_t arr[]) { k = k + 10; arr[2] = arr[2] + 10; } /* main: */ int32_t k = 1; int32_t nums[3] = {4, 5, 6}; change(k, nums); — k is passed by value, so main’s k is unchanged. The array is passed as a pointer, so nums[2] becomes 16 in main.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames

title: Mastery: CL05 · $PATH, globbing, regex, find & grep
text: How the shell finds a command, how globs expand before a command runs, how regular expressions match text, and how find and grep use them. A command containing a slash ( ./hello , ../bin/hello , /usr/bin/hello ) is a path : run exactly that file. A command with no slash ( hello , ls ) makes the shell search $PATH . $PATH is a colon-separated list of directories searched left to right; first match wins . To make your own program win, prepend its directory: export PATH="/home/me/project:$PATH" . The current directory is deliberately not on PATH: otherwise a malicious file named ls in a downloaded folder could run instead of the real one. ./ says “yes, I mean this one.” Globbing is filename expansion by the shell, before the command runs : * any characters, ? exactly one, [abc] / [a-z] one from a set or range. cat *.txt becomes cat dog.txt notes.txt ; cat never sees the star. Regex is a pattern a program uses to match text: classes [abc] , quantifiers * + ? {n} {n,} {n,m} , anchors ^ $ , and \ to escape ( . means any one character, \. a literal dot). Glob vs regex: any sequence is * vs .* ; any one char ? vs . ; literal dot . vs \. . find -name takes a glob (quote it); grep takes a regex (use -E for {n,m} , + , ? ). Common trap: Typing hello for a program in the current directory. No slash means a PATH search, which does not look in . . Common trap: Appending to PATH when you needed to prepend: a directory at the end loses to any earlier match. Common trap: An unquoted glob in find -name *.c : the shell expands it first, so find receives file names instead of a pattern. Write -name "*.c" . Common trap: grep "_[0-9]{2}$" without -E treats the braces literally and matches nothing. Common trap: Un-anchored regexes match inside longer text: ID-[0-9]{3} matches abcID-123xyz ; ^ID-[0-9]{3}$ does not.

title: Mastery: Number systems & binary arithmetic
text: Bits, hex, unsigned vs two’s complement, ranges, addition, overflow, and extension. Everything later (bitwise, types, memory) assumes this is automatic. A bit pattern has no meaning on its own . Unsigned, two’s complement and ASCII are three lenses on the same bits. Casting and printf specifiers change the lens, never the bits. An n-bit type holds exactly 2 n patterns. Unsigned: 0 to 2 n −1. Two’s complement: −2 n−1 to 2 n−1 −1 (one more negative than positive). Negate in two’s complement: flip every bit, then add 1. The MSB is the sign: 1 means negative. Two’s complement addition is the same circuit as unsigned addition. Only the overflow rule differs: unsigned = carry out of the top column; signed = result sign makes no sense for the operand signs. Widening: sign-extend signed values (copy the MSB), zero-extend unsigned values. Using the wrong one changes the value. One hex digit = exactly 4 bits, so hex is a lossless shorthand for binary (and why addresses print in hex). Common trap: Reading bits left-to-right as if the leftmost were bit 0. Bit 0 is the rightmost (LSB). Common trap: Applying the unsigned carry-out rule to signed addition (or the reverse). Common trap: Believing mixed-sign addition can overflow. It cannot: the true sum lies between the operands. Common trap: Forgetting that −128 has no positive twin in 8 bits: negating it gives itself. Common trap: Zero-extending a negative number. 1111_1101 widened with zeros is 253 , not −3.

title: Mastery: Binary & arithmetic
text: Which bit is bit 0, and what is it called? — The rightmost bit, the least significant bit (LSB). The leftmost bit of an n-bit number is bit n−1, the MSB.

title: Mastery: Binary & arithmetic
text: How many bits does one hex digit represent? — Exactly 4 . So a byte is two hex digits.

title: Mastery: Binary & arithmetic
text: Range of an n-bit unsigned integer? — 0 to 2 n − 1. (8 bits: 0 to 255.)

title: Mastery: Binary & arithmetic
text: Range of an n-bit two’s complement integer? — −2 n−1 to 2 n−1 − 1. (8 bits: −128 to 127.) One more negative than positive.

title: Mastery: Binary & arithmetic
text: Shortcut to negate a two’s complement number? — Flip all bits, then add 1. ( ~x + 1 )

title: Mastery: Binary & arithmetic
text: What is wrong with one’s complement? — Two representations of zero (all 0s and all 1s). Two’s complement reclaims that wasted pattern.

title: Mastery: Binary & arithmetic
text: How do you tell the sign of a two’s complement number? — The MSB: 0 positive, 1 negative.

title: Mastery: Binary & arithmetic
text: Sign extension vs zero extension? — Sign extension copies the MSB into the new leading bits (signed values). Zero extension fills with 0s (unsigned values).

title: Mastery: Binary & arithmetic
text: How is unsigned overflow detected when adding? — The carry-out of the most significant column is 1.

title: Mastery: Binary & arithmetic
text: How is two’s complement overflow detected? — Same-sign operands give a result of the opposite sign (pos+pos = negative, neg+neg = positive). Mixed-sign addition never overflows.

title: Mastery: Binary & arithmetic
text: Same 32 bits printed with %d and %u differ. Why? — The bits are identical. %d reads them as signed two’s complement, %u as unsigned.

title: Mastery: Binary & arithmetic

title: Mastery: Binary & arithmetic
text: How do you convert a decimal number to binary by hand? — Repeatedly subtract the largest power of 2 that fits, writing a 1 in that position. Unused positions are 0.

title: Mastery: Binary & arithmetic
text: What decimal value is 0b1011 ? — 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11.

title: Mastery: Binary & arithmetic
text: Why is hex used for memory addresses and raw bytes? — The 4-bits-per-digit mapping is exact, so hex is compact and easy to convert.

title: Mastery: Binary & arithmetic
text: What is the main advantage of two’s complement over one’s complement? — Reclaiming the redundant all-ones zero gives one extra negative value and lets the same adder serve both interpretations.

title: Mastery: Binary & arithmetic

(Think: arithmetic happens in int , then the assignment narrows to the target type.) int8_t a = 127; int8_t b = a + 1; uint8_t c = b; int32_t d = b; — 127 + 1 = 128, which narrows into int8_t as −128 (bits 1000_0000). c reinterprets those bits as unsigned: 128. d sign-extends the signed b : −128.
