text: Explain why two’s complement lets one adder circuit do both signed and unsigned addition, and how the two overflow rules differ. — The adder just adds bits and carries; whether the pattern means unsigned or two’s complement is only the interpretation afterwards. Because of how negatives are encoded, a + (−a) wraps to zero. What differs is only how we detect that the true answer did not fit.

title: Mastery: Binary & arithmetic
text: You widen an 8-bit value to 32 bits. Explain when to sign-extend, when to zero-extend, and what goes wrong if you pick the wrong one. — Widening must preserve the number you meant. For signed values that means repeating the sign bit; for unsigned values the new high bits are plain zeros. Mixing them up changes the value.

title: Mastery: Bitwise operators, shifts & masks
text: AND, OR, XOR, NOT, shifts, and the get / set / clear / update / pack / extract idioms built from them. Bitwise ( & | ^ ~ ) work one bit position at a time and return a same-width result. Logical ( && || ! ) collapse each operand to one truth value first. The mask toolkit: get num & mask · set num | mask · clear num & ~mask · toggle num ^ mask , with mask = 1 << i . Left shift fills with 0s and equals ×2 per shift unless bits fall off the top. Bits shifted out are lost, never wrapped. Right shift depends on the type : unsigned is logical (0s in), signed is usually arithmetic (copies the sign bit). To write a field: clear first, then OR . OR can only turn bits on. To read a field: shift down, then mask . ~x only makes sense once you know the width of x . Common trap: Writing && when you meant & (and the reverse). 5 & 2 is 0 but 5 && 2 is 1. Common trap: Precedence: == binds tighter than & . num & 1 << i == 0 does not mean what it looks like. Parenthesize. Common trap: Cast order: (uint8_t)(d >> 1) and (uint8_t)d >> 1 give different results because the first shifts arithmetically , the second logically . Common trap: Using update_bit = num | (x << i) : it can never write a 0 into a bit that is already 1. Common trap: Assuming bits shifted off the left “wrap around.” They are discarded.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: When is each bit of a & b , a | b , a ^ b equal to 1? — AND: both bits 1. OR: at least one is 1. XOR: exactly one is 1 (the bits differ).

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: & vs && ? — & works bit by bit and returns a same-width number. && collapses each side to true/false and returns 0 or 1. 5 & 2 = 0 , 5 && 2 = 1 .

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: Build a mask with a single 1 at bit i. — 1 << i

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: Get / set / clear / toggle bit i of num . — get: (num & (1<<i)) != 0 · set: num | (1<<i) · clear: num & ~(1<<i) · toggle: num ^ (1<<i)

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: Why does update_bit clear before OR-ing? — OR can only turn bits on. If bit i is 1 and x is 0, plain OR leaves it 1. Clear it, then OR in x << i .

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: What fills in on a left shift? On a right shift? — Left: always 0s on the right. Right: 0s if the value is unsigned (logical); a copy of the sign bit if signed (arithmetic).

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: What happens to bits shifted off either end? — They are discarded. Nothing wraps around.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: x << n equals what arithmetic, and when does it break? — Multiplication by 2 n , unless significant bits fall off the top of the fixed width.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: Multiply n by 20 using only shifts and addition. — (n << 4) + (n << 2) since 20 = 16 + 4.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: Pack two 4-bit values into one byte. — (high << 4) | low

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: Extract the green byte from 0xRRGGBB . — (color >> 8) & 0xFF (shift into position, then mask).

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: Why is ~x ambiguous without a width? — ~ flips every bit, and how many bits there are depends on the type of x .

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: Precedence trap: num & 1 << i == 0 ? — == binds tighter than & , so it is num & ((1<<i) == 0) . Always parenthesize: (num & (1<<i)) == 0 .

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: What do 5 & 2 and 5 && 2 evaluate to? — Bitwise AND sees 101 and 010 share no set bit (0). Logical AND sees two nonzero values (1).

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: A bit position of a ^ b is 1 exactly when… — XOR detects difference: 0^0 = 0, 1^1 = 0, 0^1 = 1.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: Which expression clears bit i of num and leaves every other bit alone? — ~(1<<i) is all 1s except position i, so the AND zeroes only that bit.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: With int8_t d = -2; , what is d >> 1 ? — 1111_1110 shifted right arithmetically copies the sign bit: 1111_1111 = −1.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: What does this print? uint8_t a = 0b00101101; uint8_t b = a << 2; printf("%d", b); — 0010_1101 shifted left twice is 1011_0100 = 180 (= 45 × 4). Nothing fell off, so it equals ×4.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: What does this print? uint8_t a = 0b11001101; uint8_t b = a << 2; printf("%d", b); — 1100_1101 << 2 would need 10 bits; the top two (11) are discarded, leaving 0011_0100 = 52. This is why “×2” fails once bits fall off.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: Both d and u hold the same bits 1110_1100 . Fill in each result. int8_t d = -20; uint8_t u = 236; int r1 = d >> 2; int r2 = u >> 2; — Signed d shifts arithmetically: 1111_1011 = −5. Unsigned u shifts logically: 0011_1011 = 59. Same bits, different shift, because the type decides.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: With int8_t d = -2; (bits 1111_1110), what do these print as decimal? int8_t d = -2; int a = (uint8_t)(d >> 1); int b = (uint8_t)(d) >> 1; — a : shift first on the signed value (arithmetic, 1111_1111), then cast: 255. b : cast first (254), then a logical shift: 0111_1111 = 127.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: For 4-bit values 1100 and 1010 , give the 4-bit result of each operator. — Column by column: AND keeps positions where both are 1; OR keeps any 1; XOR keeps positions that differ.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: Given num = 0b0110_1001 (105), find the decimal result of each, each applied to the original num . int8_t num = 0b01101001; int s = num | (1 << 1); int c = num & ~(1 << 0); int t = num ^ (1 << 6); — s: 0110_1001 | 0000_0010 = 0110_1011 = 107. c: clear bit 0 gives 0110_1000 = 104. t: flip bit 6 gives 0010_1001 = 41.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: update_bit(num, i, x) should set bit i to x (0 or 1), but update_bit(0b0101, 2, 0) returns 5, not 1. Find the root cause. — The mask is computed and then ignored. Apply it first ( num & mask ), then OR in x << i .

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: is_clear(5, 1) should return 1 (bit 1 of 0b101 is 0) but returns 0. Which line is the root cause? — Precedence: shifts, then == , then & . Write (num & (1 << i)) == 0 .

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: Arrange a correct update_bit . Two lines do not belong. — Clear bit i with AND (using the inverted mask), then OR the new value into position i. Using OR to clear or AND to set reverses the roles.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: Pack two 4-bit values into one byte, high nibble first. uint8_t packed = (high __0__ 4) __1__ low; — Shift the high nibble into the top four bits, then OR in the low nibble. The low nibble only occupies the bottom four bits, so nothing collides.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: Using only shifts and addition, multiply n by 20 (20 = 16 + 4). Put the larger shift first. n = (n << __0__) + (n << __1__); — n << 4 is ×16 and n << 2 is ×4; 16 + 4 = 20.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: This function brightens the blue channel of a packed 0xRRGGBB color, clamping at 0xFF. Give each output as hex (e.g. 0x1020FF ). uint32_t cool(uint32_t c) { uint32_t blue = c & 0xFF; uint32_t nb = (blue + 0x30 > 0xFF) ? 0xFF : blue + 0x30; return (c & 0xFFFF00) | nb; } — 0xF0 + 0x30 = 0x120 overflows a byte, so it clamps to 0xFF (0x1020FF). 0x00 + 0x30 = 0x30 fits (0x10EE30). Clearing the old blue ( c & 0xFFFF00 ) before OR-ing is the same clear-then-set pattern as update_bit.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: Fill in the decimal value of each variable. uint8_t packed = (0b0101 > 4; uint8_t lo = packed & 0x0F; — packed = 0101_1100 = 92. Shifting right by 4 recovers 0101 = 5. Masking with 0x0F keeps the low nibble 1100 = 12. Pack and unpack are exact inverses.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: What does this print? int n = 5; n = (n << 4) + (n << 2); printf("%d", n); — 5 × 16 + 5 × 4 = 80 + 20 = 100, which is 5 × 20.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: You must overwrite just the middle four bits (bits 5 to 2) of a byte b with a 4-bit value v , leaving the other bits alone. Which is correct? — 0x3C is 0011_1100, the field. b & ~0x3C clears it, v << 2 moves the new value into place, OR merges. Clear first, then set.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: Write int count_ones(uint8_t x) that returns how many bits of x are 1, using only shifts and masks (no library calls). Say why your loop terminates correctly for every input, including 0 and 255. — int count_ones(uint8_t x) { int count = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { count += (x >> i) & 1; } return count; } It examines each of the 8 bit positions exactly once, so it terminates for every input. Shifting right and masking with 1 reads bit i; summing those reads counts the set bits.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: Explain how to overwrite a multi-bit field inside an integer, and why you must clear the old field before OR-ing in the new value. — Clear the field with num & ~mask , then merge with | (v << shift) . Skipping the clear lets old 1 bits survive the OR.

title: Mastery: Bitwise & masks
text: A friend says “ >> divides by two.” Explain exactly what a right shift does, including what changes between unsigned and signed values and what happens to bits that fall off. — A shift slides all bits right; the ones that fall off are lost. The type decides what enters on the left: 0s for unsigned, a copy of the sign bit for signed. That is why -2 >> 1 is -1 but the same bits as unsigned give 127.

title: Mastery: Unix shell, redirection, globbing & $PATH
text: The file system tree, paths, core commands, the three standard streams, pipes, globbing vs regex, how commands are found, and environment variables. The shell (bash) interprets your commands; the terminal only displays text. The shell does expansion before the program runs : globs, $VAR and ~ are replaced first, and the program sees only the result. Every process has three streams: 0 stdin , 1 stdout , 2 stderr . > overwrites, >> appends, 2> redirects stderr, < feeds stdin, and | connects one command’s stdout to the next one’s stdin (no file). Globbing (shell, matches filenames ): * any run, ? exactly one char, [abc] / [a-z] one of a set. Regex (a program like grep, matches text ) adds + ? {n,m} ^ $ and needs .* for “any run.” Typing a command name makes the shell search $PATH (colon-separated) left to right, first match wins . The current directory is not searched, hence ./prog . A variable is visible to child processes only if exported . Use $VAR to expand, and ${VAR} when text follows the name. Absolute paths start at / ; everything else is relative to the current directory. . is here, .. is the parent, ~ is home. rm has no undo. Common trap: Re-running a command with > destroys the previous output. Use >> to keep it. Common trap: Setting PATH=“/some/dir” replaces it. Append with PATH=“$PATH:/some/dir” or every command disappears. Common trap: * means different things: alone in a glob it is “any characters”; in a regex it means “zero or more of the previous thing.” Common trap: NAME=x without export is invisible to a child shell or program. Common trap: find -name takes a glob , not a regex. Quote it so the shell does not expand it first.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Terminal vs shell vs CLI? — Terminal = the window/app that shows text. Shell (bash) = the program that interprets and runs commands. CLI = the text-based style of interaction.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Absolute vs relative path? — Absolute starts at / . Relative starts from the current working directory. . here, .. parent, ~ home.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: cp vs mv ? — cp leaves the source and makes a copy. mv removes it from the old place (and is also how you rename). Neither changes your cwd.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: rmdir vs rm -r ? — rmdir only removes an empty directory (a safety net). rm -r removes a directory and everything in it, with no undo.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: The three standard streams? — 0 = stdin (keyboard), 1 = stdout, 2 = stderr (both terminal by default).

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: > vs >> vs 2> vs < ? — > overwrite stdout to a file · >> append · 2> redirect stderr · < read stdin from a file.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: What does a | b do? — Connects a’s stdout directly to b’s stdin. No file is written.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Which stream do printf / putchar write to? How do you write to stderr? — stdout always. Use fprintf(stderr, ...) or fputc(c, stderr) .

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Glob wildcards? — * any run (incl. empty) · ? exactly one char · [abc] one of the set · [a-z] a range.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Who evaluates a glob? A regex? — A glob is expanded by the shell against filenames, before the command runs. A regex is evaluated by a program (grep) against text.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Regex pieces: ^ $ * + ? {n,m} — start of line · end of line · zero or more · one or more · zero or one · between n and m of the previous thing. “Any run” is .* .

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: How does the shell find a command? — It searches each directory in $PATH (colon-separated), left to right, first match wins. The current directory is not searched.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Why do you type ./prog ? — . is not on $PATH (deliberately, so a rogue file named ls cannot hijack the real one). ./ names the file explicitly.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Make a shell variable visible to child processes? — export VAR (or export VAR=value ). Plain assignment is not inherited.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: $VAR vs ${VAR} vs VAR ? — VAR is the literal text. $VAR expands. ${VAR} expands with explicit boundaries, needed when text follows ( ${VAR}file ).

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Which of these is an absolute path? — An absolute path starts at the root / and means the same thing from anywhere.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: You run ./run > log.txt twice. What does log.txt contain? — > truncates then writes; >> appends.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: You compile to hello in your current directory and type hello . The shell says “command not found.” Why? — Type ./hello to name the file explicitly.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Who interprets the pattern in ls *.c versus grep '^a.*z$' f.txt ? — Globs are shell expansion before the command runs. Regexes are the program’s job.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: In a shell you run export A=1 and B=2 , then start bash . In the child shell, which are set? — Only exported variables are inherited by child processes.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: The directory holds lab.c lab0.c lab1.c lab10.c labX.c notes.txt . What does echo lab?.c print? — ? matches exactly one character: “0”, “1”, “X”. lab.c has none and lab10.c has two.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Same directory. What does echo lab[01]*.c print? (Names in alphabetical order, space separated.) — [01] is one character, 0 or 1; * then matches any run, including none. lab.c and labX.c fail the [01] position.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: How many lines does f.txt have at the end? echo a > f.txt echo b >> f.txt echo c > f.txt echo d >> f.txt cat f.txt | grep -c . — The third command uses > , which truncates the file, wiping a and b. Then d is appended: the file is c, d.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: With names.txt containing ab_12, ab_123, AB_12, a_1, xyz_99 (one per line), which two lines does grep -E '^[a-z]+_[0-9]{2}$' names.txt print, in file order? — ^[a-z]+ is one or more lowercase letters, _ , then exactly two digits, then end of line. ab_123 has three digits, AB_12 is uppercase, a_1 has one digit.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: What does this print? (Note the exact text.) export A=1 B=2 bash -c 'echo "A=$A B=$B"' — The child bash inherits the exported A but not B , which was a plain shell variable. $B expands to nothing.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: With NAME=data , what does echo $NAMEfile ${NAME}file print? — $NAMEfile looks up a variable called NAMEfile , which does not exist, so it expands to nothing and vanishes. ${NAME}file uses braces to end the name: datafile .

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: A script is meant to collect results from two test runs into results.txt , but only the second run’s output is there. Find the root cause. — Use >> on the second line to append.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: After sourcing this .bashrc , ls and gcc stop working (“command not found”). Which line is responsible? — Write export PATH="$PATH:/home/me/bin" . The old value is referenced with $PATH so nothing is lost.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Count the lines of log.txt that contain the word error . Fill the operator that sends grep’s output into wc -l . grep error log.txt __0__ wc -l — The pipe connects grep’s stdout to wc’s stdin, with no temporary file.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Send a program’s normal output to out.txt and its error messages to err.txt . ./prog __0__ out.txt __1__ err.txt — > redirects stdout (fd 1); 2> redirects stderr (fd 2).

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Files: a.txt a1.txt a2.txt a10.txt . Which pattern matches exactly a1.txt and a2.txt ? — ? demands exactly one character, which rules out a.txt (none) and a10.txt (two).

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: The program p prints ok to stdout and bad to stderr. After ./p > out.txt 2> err.txt , what does each file contain? (The terminal shows nothing.) — Each stream was redirected to its own file, so nothing reaches the terminal.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Same program p . How many lines does grep -c . count in each case? — 2>&1 sends stderr to wherever stdout goes (the pipe), so both lines are counted. Without it only stdout enters the pipe; bad goes straight to the terminal.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text:
What does this print? printf 'b
a
b
c
a
' > in.txt sort in.txt | uniq | grep -c . — sort groups equal lines (a a b b c), uniq collapses adjacent duplicates (a b c), and grep -c . counts the non-empty lines: 3.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Select all true statements. — Globs are filename expansion by the shell; regexes are matched by a program. They share the character-class syntax but differ in what * means.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Write a single shell command that prints how many .c files in the current directory contain the word main . Then say, for each part, who processes it (shell or a program) and what it does. — grep -l main *.c | wc -l *.c is expanded by the shell into the list of filenames before grep starts. grep -l main prints the names of the files that contain “main”, one per line. The | feeds that list to wc -l , which counts the lines, i.e. the files.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Explain the difference between a glob and a regular expression, including who evaluates each and what * means in each. — The shell turns *.c into filenames and the command never sees the pattern. A regex is data the program itself interprets over text. The star is a wildcard in globs but a quantifier in regex.

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Explain how the shell finds the program when you type foo , why you need ./ for your own program, and what can go wrong when you edit $PATH . — Command lookup is a left-to-right scan of the directories in $PATH, stopping at the first executable with that name. The current directory is deliberately not on it. Editing PATH must keep the old value ( PATH=“$PATH:…” ).

title: Mastery: Shell & Unix
text: Explain the difference between a shell variable and an environment variable, and what a child process (like a program you launch) can see. — Exporting marks the variable to be copied into the environment of any process the shell starts. Unexported ones stay local, and a child only ever gets a copy.

title: Mastery: C fundamentals: types, ASCII, arrays & strings
text: How C source becomes a program, what types and printf mean, characters as numbers, arrays without lengths, null-terminated strings, and the getchar/EOF input loop. Four stages: preprocessor ( #include , #define : pure text substitution) → compiler (C to assembly) → assembler (to a .o object file) → linker (adds library code, produces the executable). gcc hello.c does all four and runs nothing ; you run ./a.out . A type decides how many bytes a value takes and what its bits mean . The same byte is 65 or 'A' depending on how you read it. A char is a small integer. c - '0' turns a digit character into its value; c + ('a'-'A') is a case change. Escape sequences like \n are one character. A C array does not know its own length and is not bounds-checked: reading or writing past the end is undefined behavior. Pass the size separately. A string is a char array ending in '\0' . sizeof is the declared size (compile time, includes unused space and the null); strlen counts up to the first null (run time). getchar() returns an int so it can also return EOF (−1), which no real byte can equal. Store it in an int , not a char . Common trap: Thinking gcc file.c runs the program, or trying to run the .c source file. Common trap: Storing getchar() in a char : EOF becomes indistinguishable from a valid byte. Common trap: ndigit[c]++ instead of ndigit[c - '0']++ : c is an ASCII code like 53, far past a 10-element array. Common trap: Forgetting the null terminator when sizing a buffer: "abc" needs 4 bytes. Common trap: Expecting sizeof to be the string length, or strlen to be the array size.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: The four stages from .c to executable? — Preprocessor ( #include / #define text expansion) → compiler (to assembly) → assembler (to object code, .o ) → linker (combine with library code).

title: Mastery: C basics
text: Does gcc hello.c run the program? — No. It builds a.out (silence means success). Run it with ./a.out . -o name picks the output name.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: What does main ’s return value mean? — The exit status: 0 means success, non-zero means some failure.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: Why #include <stdio.h> ? — It supplies the declarations (name, return type, parameters) so the compiler can check calls to printf, getchar, etc. C includes nothing automatically.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: #define vs a const variable? — #define is text substitution before compiling: no memory, no type. A const is a real, typed variable.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: What does a C array not have, compared to Java? — No .length and no bounds checking. Out-of-bounds access is undefined behavior; pass the size separately.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: How is a C string stored? — As a char array ending in '\0' (the null terminator). "abc" takes 4 bytes.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: sizeof vs strlen ? — sizeof: declared array size, compile time, includes the null and spare room. strlen: characters before the first null, run time.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: Convert a digit char to its number, and back. — c - '0' and n + '0' (ASCII digits are consecutive, '0' = 48).

title: Mastery: C basics
text: ASCII anchors worth knowing? — '0' =48, 'A' =65, 'a' =97, space=32, '\n' =10, '\0' =0. Lowercase minus uppercase = 32.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: Why is getchar() stored in an int ? — It returns every byte value 0–255 and EOF (−1). A char cannot hold both, so EOF could be confused with a real byte.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: printf placeholders to know? — %d int · %u unsigned · %c char · %s string · %x hex · %f float · %zu size_t.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: What does int division do? — Truncates toward zero: 7/2 is 3. 7 % 2 is 1. Use 7/2.0 for 3.5.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: Typical sizes? — char 1 · short 2 · int 4 · long 8 (usually) · pointer 8 on this architecture. int32_t etc. fix the size exactly.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: Which stage expands #define and pastes in #include files? — The preprocessor runs first and handles every line beginning with # as pure text manipulation.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: You run gcc hello.c and nothing prints. What happened? — Compiling and running are separate steps. Silence is how gcc says it succeeded.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: Why should c be an int in while ((c = getchar()) != EOF) ? — If c were a char , the byte 0xFF could be mistaken for EOF (or EOF never matched on some platforms).

title: Mastery: C basics
text: In C, what does a function receive when you pass an array int a[10] ? — This is why C functions taking arrays also take a size parameter.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: Select all true statements about char s[] = "abc"; — The literal needs 3 characters plus a terminating null = 4 bytes. strlen stops before the null.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: What does this print? (four numbers separated by spaces) char s[] = "211"; char t[20] = "hi"; printf("%zu %zu %zu %zu", sizeof(s), strlen(s), sizeof(t), strlen(t)); — s has 3 characters + null = 4 bytes and strlen 3. t is declared 20 bytes; "hi" fills 2, so strlen 2.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: What does this print? (format: text|number|number) char str[] = {'U','N','C','\0','t','a'}; printf("%s|%zu|%zu", str, strlen(str), sizeof(str)); — %s and strlen stop at the first null (after UNC), so 3 characters print. sizeof is the whole array: 6.

title: Mastery: C basics
text:
Fill in what each printf prints. char c = '7'; printf("%d
", c - '0'); printf("%c
", 'a' + 2); printf("%c
", 'g' - ('a' - 'A')); — '7' is 55 and '0' is 48, so 7. 'a' + 2 is 'c'. Lowercase is 32 above uppercase, so subtracting ('a'-'A') uppercases 'g' to 'G'.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: What does this print? (format: three values) printf("%d %d %.2f", 7 / 2, 7 % 2, 7 / 2.0); — Integer division truncates (3), % gives the remainder (1), and a double operand makes the division floating point (3.50).

title: Mastery: C basics
text: What does this print? printf("%d %x %c %s", 65, 255, 65, "hi"); — %d prints 65, %x prints 255 in hex (ff), %c reinterprets 65 as the character A, %s prints the string.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: The loop below runs over the text a1b22c333 . Fill in the final ndigit entries. int ndigit[10] = {0}; for (char *p = "a1b22c333"; *p; p++) { int c = *p; if (c >= '0' && c <= '9') ++ndigit[c - '0']; } — Letters fail the range test. '1' appears once, '2' twice, '3' three times. c - '0' maps each digit character to its own index.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: This loop sometimes stops early on binary input (or never stops on some machines). Which line is the root cause? — getchar returns an int covering 256 byte values plus EOF. Narrowing to char loses that.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: This code zeroes an array but sometimes corrupts a neighboring variable. Find the bug. — Valid indices are 0 to 4. Use i < 5 . Out-of-bounds writes are undefined behavior and can silently overwrite other memory.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: strcpy sometimes crashes or corrupts nearby data here. Which line is wrong? — A string of length n needs n + 1 bytes. strcpy writes the null at dest[3] , one past the end.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: This counts each digit character but crashes or gives garbage. Find the root cause. — Index with c - '0' , and only when c is between '0' and '9'.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: Arrange the loop that counts digit characters from stdin. One line does not belong. — Read until EOF, test that c is a digit character, and index with c - '0' so '5' (53) lands at slot 5.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: Compile hello.c into an executable named hello , then run it. gcc hello.c __0__ hello __1__hello — -o hello names the output; ./hello runs it, with ./ because the current directory is not on $PATH.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: Fill in the output pieces. char s[] = "hello"; for (int i = 0; s[i] != '\0'; i++) { if (s[i] >= 'a' && s[i] <= 'z') s[i] -= 'a' - 'A'; } printf("%s %zu %zu", s, strlen(s), sizeof(s)); — Each lowercase letter drops by 32, giving HELLO. Case changes do not alter length: strlen 5; sizeof is 6 with the null.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: What does this print? (format: text number) char buf[8] = "ab"; buf[2] = 'c'; printf("%s %zu", buf, strlen(buf)); — A partial initializer zero-fills the remainder, so buf[2] through buf[7] start as null. Overwriting buf[2] with 'c' leaves buf[3] as a null, so the string is now "abc".

title: Mastery: C basics
text: Fill in the values. char dest[20]; strcpy(dest, "211"); size_t a = sizeof(dest); size_t b = strlen(dest); char c = dest[3]; — dest is declared 20 bytes, so sizeof is 20 regardless of content. strcpy copies "211" and the null, so strlen is 3 and dest[3] is the terminator (0).

title: Mastery: C basics
text: Which statement prints exactly He said "hi" followed by a newline? — Each \" is one literal quote character and \n is one newline character.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: Write int count_char(const char *s, char c) that returns how many times c appears in the string s . Do not call strlen . Explain how your loop knows when to stop. — int count_char(const char *s, char c) { int count = 0; for (int i = 0; s[i] != '\0'; i++) { if (s[i] == c) count++; } return count; } The loop stops at the null terminator, because a C string has no stored length, only the '\0' that ends it.

title: Mastery: C basics
text:
Write a complete C program that reads all of stdin and prints how many lines it contained (count the '
' characters). Include everything needed to compile. — #include <stdio.h> int main(void) { int c, lines = 0; while ((c = getchar()) != EOF) { if (c == '
') lines++; } printf("%d
", lines); return 0; }

title: Mastery: C basics
text: Explain what happens between hello.c and a running program, naming each stage, what it produces, and why gcc hello.c prints nothing. — Four stages: preprocess, compile, assemble, link. gcc runs all four in one command and stops. The program only executes when you run the file it produced.

title: Mastery: C basics
text: Explain how C represents a string, the difference between sizeof and strlen , and why C functions that take arrays also take a size. — The data is just bytes. A null byte marks where a string ends. sizeof reports the container, strlen reports the string inside it. Since the array does not know its own length, callers pass one.

title: Mastery: Stack frames, pointers & pass-by-value
text: What a function call physically does to memory, what is copied versus shared, and how a pointer lets a callee reach back into its caller. The single most exam-relevant mental model in the course. Every call pushes a stack frame holding the return address (where to resume in the caller), the arguments , and the locals . Returning pops it: sp moves back and that memory is dead. A frame field is either a copy or an address . Copies (all plain scalars) cannot affect the caller. Addresses (pointers) can, because writing through one reaches the caller’s memory. Arrays are never copied into a callee. An array parameter is an 8-byte pointer to the caller’s array (it “decays”), so arr[i]++ changes the caller’s data while size = 0 does not. All pointers are 8 bytes on this architecture, whatever they point to. &x is x’s address, *p follows the address. p + 1 moves one element , not one byte. The most recently called, not-yet-returned function is always on top ( last in, first out ). Locals die with their frame, so never return the address of a local. sizeof on an array parameter is the size of a pointer (8), not of the array: it has already decayed. Common trap: Believing the callee gets its own copy of an array. It gets an address . Common trap: Returning &local or a local array: the frame is gone when the function returns. Common trap: Writing *t++ when you meant (*t)++ : the first advances the pointer . Common trap: Passing a variable ( swap(x, y) ) when the callee needs its address ( swap(&x, &y) ). Common trap: Using sizeof(arr) for an array parameter to get its length.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: Name the three things inside a stack frame. — Return address (RA), arguments, local variables.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: What does the return address store? — The address in the caller where execution resumes after the callee returns. Not the return value .

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: What happens to sp on a call? On a return? — Call: a frame is pushed and sp moves to make room. Return: the frame is popped and sp moves back. Last in, first out.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: A function takes int32_t arr[5] . What lands in its frame? — An 8-byte pointer to the caller’s array. The array is never copied, so writes through arr change the caller’s data.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: Why does size = 0; in a callee not affect the caller’s size ? — Scalars are passed by value : the callee has its own copy in its own frame.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: How big is any pointer here? — 8 bytes, whatever it points to.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: Why is returning &local a bug? — The local lives in the callee’s frame, which is popped on return. The pointer then refers to dead memory.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: How do you let a function change the caller’s int ? — Pass its address ( &x ) and write through the pointer parameter ( *p = … ).

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: sizeof(arr) inside a function where arr is an array parameter? — The size of a pointer (8), not the array. It decayed on the way in. Pass the length separately.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: The one question to ask about every parameter? — “Is this a copy , or an address back into the caller?”

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: What does p + 1 do for an int32_t *p ? — Advances the address by 4 bytes (one element). Pointer arithmetic is scaled by the pointee size.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: *p++ vs (*p)++ ? — *p++ reads the value and then advances the pointer . (*p)++ increments the value p points to.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: Which function’s frame is on top of the stack? — The most recently called function that has not yet returned.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: In void f(int32_t arr[5]) , what does the parameter arr actually hold? — The array decays to a pointer: 8 bytes holding the address of the caller’s data.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: After a function returns, what has happened to its stack frame? — Returning pops the frame; that memory is reused by the next call.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: On this architecture, how many bytes does a char * occupy? — Every pointer is an address: 8 bytes whatever the pointee type.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: Select all things stored in a function’s own stack frame. — Return address, arguments and locals. Anything else the callee touches is reached through an address.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: What does this program print? (two numbers separated by a space) void bump(int32_t x, int32_t *p) { x = x + 1; *p = *p + 1; } int main(void) { int32_t a = 5, b = 5; bump(a, &b); printf("%d %d", a, b); } — x is a copy of a (a stays 5). p holds &b , so *p writes to main’s b.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: Fill in main ’s variables after scale returns. void scale(int32_t a[], int32_t n) { for (int32_t i = 0; i < n; i++) { a[i] *= 2; } n = 0; } int main(void) { int32_t arr[3] = {4, 5, 6}; int32_t n = 3; scale(arr, n); } — The array is shared (writes go through the pointer), so all three double. n was copied, so n = 0 only changed the callee’s copy.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: Using the lesson’s sizes (return address 8 bytes, pointer 8, int32_t 4; ignore padding), how many bytes is scale ’s stack frame above, including its local i ? — RA 8 + a (a pointer) 8 + n 4 + i 4 = 24 . The array’s 12 bytes are not in this frame; they live in main’s.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: Fill in the final state. ( &v[1] is the address of the second element.) void inc_all(int32_t *p, int32_t n) { for (int32_t i = 0; i < n; i++) p[i]++; } int main(void) { int32_t v[3] = {1, 2, 3}; int32_t k = 3; inc_all(v, k); inc_all(&v[1], 2); } — After the first call v = {2, 3, 4}. The second call starts at &v[1] and increments two elements: v[1] and v[2], giving {2, 4, 5}. k is a copy and never changes.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: Fill in the values after these statements. int32_t a[3] = {10, 20, 30}; int32_t *p = a; int32_t x = *p++; int32_t y = (*p)++; — *p++ reads a[0] (10) and then moves p to a[1]. (*p)++ then reads a[1] (20) and increments the value there to 21.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: Fill in the two printed lines. void swap_v(int32_t a, int32_t b) { int32_t t = a; a = b; b = t; } void swap_p(int32_t *a, int32_t *b) { int32_t t = *a; *a = *b; *b = t; } int main(void) { int32_t x = 1, y = 2; swap_v(x, y); printf("%d %d\n", x, y); // line 1 swap_p(&x, &y); printf("%d %d\n", x, y); // line 2 } — swap_v swaps its own copies, so nothing changes in main. swap_p swaps the values at the addresses, so main’s variables really swap.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: This function is supposed to hand back a counter. Callers sometimes see garbage. Find the root cause. — count lives in make_counter ’s frame. On return that frame is popped, so the returned address refers to dead memory.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: name() sometimes returns garbled text. Which line is the root cause? — The array is destroyed with the frame. The caller should pass in a buffer to fill instead.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: swap(x, y) is called from main, but x and y never change. Which line is the root cause? — Pass-by-value gives swap its own copies. To change the caller’s variables you must pass their addresses .

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: Arrange the lines into a swap that actually works. Two lines do not belong. — Save *a in a temp, copy *b into *a , then the temp into *b . Every access goes through the pointers.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: Fill the two blanks so clear sets every element of the caller’s array to 0. void clear(int32_t __0__, int32_t n) { for (int32_t i = 0; i < n; i++) { __1__ = 0; } } — The parameter is a[] (or *a ), and the write is a[i] = 0 , which reaches the caller’s memory through the pointer.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: Two functions, one shared array, and a fixed-size type. Fill in main’s values after both calls. ( int8_t holds −128..127 and wraps.) int8_t total(int8_t *v, int32_t n) { int8_t s = 0; for (int32_t i = 0; i < n; i++) { s += v[i]; } return s; } void double_all(int8_t v[], int32_t n) { for (int32_t i = 0; i < n; i++) { v[i] *= 2; } } int main(void) { int8_t v[3] = {100, 50, 10}; int8_t s = total(v, 3); double_all(v, 3); } — s: 100 + 50 + 10 = 160, which wraps in 8 bits to 160 − 256 = −96 . double_all writes through the pointer into main’s array: 200 wraps to −56, then 100 and 20. Overflow, a shared array and a return value all matter.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: With char word[] = "hello"; in main, length(word) is expected to give 6 (including the null) but prints 8. Why? — The array decayed to a pointer on the way in, so inside the callee sizeof(s) is sizeof(char *) = 8. Pass the length as a parameter (or use strlen ).

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: You must write append_one(...) so that after append_one(&total) the caller’s int32_t total has increased by 1. Which works? — Take the address, and write through it with parentheses: (*t)++ .

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: This returns a pointer into main’s array (which is safe, unlike a local). Fill in the results. int32_t *max_ptr(int32_t *a, int32_t n) { int32_t *m = a; for (int32_t i = 1; i *m) m = &a[i]; } return m; } int main(void) { int32_t v[4] = {3, 9, 2, 7}; int32_t *p = max_ptr(v, 4); *p = 0; } — The maximum is 9 at index 1, so p points at v[1] and p - v is 1 element. Writing through p zeroes v[1] in main’s frame. Returning this pointer is safe because the array outlives the call.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: Write void swap_ends(int32_t *a, int32_t n) that swaps the first and last element of an array. Then say what arr contains in main after swap_ends(arr, 4) when arr = {1, 2, 3, 4} , and why main sees the change even though the function returns nothing. — void swap_ends(int32_t *a, int32_t n) { int32_t tmp = a[0]; a[0] = a[n - 1]; a[n - 1] = tmp; } arr becomes {4, 2, 3, 1} . The function received an 8-byte pointer to main’s array, so writes through a modify main’s memory directly. Nothing needs to be returned.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: Write void reverse(int32_t *a, int32_t n) that reverses the array in place (no second array). What is the loop bound and why is it safe for both even and odd n ? — void reverse(int32_t *a, int32_t n) { for (int32_t i = 0; i < n / 2; i++) { int32_t tmp = a[i]; a[i] = a[n - 1 - i]; a[n - 1 - i] = tmp; } } Loop to n/2 : each iteration swaps a pair (i, n−1−i). For odd n the middle element pairs with itself and needs no swap; integer division drops it automatically. Going to n would swap everything back.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: In the program below, describe what is on the stack at the moment g is executing *p = *p + n; : how many frames, in what order, and for each frame the fields and whether each is a copy or an address. What does main print? void g(int32_t *p, int32_t n) { *p = *p + n; } void f(int32_t k) { int32_t t = k; g(&t, 10); } int main(void) { int32_t a = 1; f(a); printf("%d", a); } — Three frames, top last: main ( a=1 ), f (RA into main; k=1 , a copy of a; local t=1 ), g (RA into f; p = address of f’s t , 8 bytes; n=10 , a copy). *p = *p + n writes f’s t (1 → 11), not main’s a. main prints 1 , because f received only a copy of a.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: Teach it. In your own words: why does arr[i]++ inside a function change the caller’s array, but size = 0 does not change the caller’s size ? Mention what is actually stored in the callee’s stack frame. — Everything in the callee’s frame is either a copy or an address . size is a copy, so setting it to 0 changes only the callee’s own variable. arr is the address of the caller’s array, so arr[i]++ reaches back into the caller’s frame and changes the real data.

title: Mastery: Stack & pointers
text: Explain why returning the address of a local variable is a bug, in terms of what happens to the stack. — The local’s storage belongs to the frame. When the function returns, the frame is popped and its bytes get reused by whatever is called next, so the saved address leads to garbage.

title: Mastery: Debugging & testing
text: Using a real debugger (breakpoints, stepping, watch), understanding I/O buffering, how the VS Code + GDB setup fits together, and designing tests that actually expose bugs. Debugging is predict, then compare : work out by hand what each variable should be after each line, then step and find the first line where actual ≠ predicted . The bug is there, or just before. A breakpoint pauses before its line executes. Step Over runs the line (including any call) as one step; Step Into enters a called function; Step Out finishes the current function. The Variables panel shows a variable by its declared type (an int holding ‘a’ shows 97). A Watch expression like (char)c re-reads the same bits as another type. Buffering: stdout text sits in memory until a newline (on a terminal), the buffer fills, fflush(stdout) , or exit. stderr is unbuffered. That is why output can appear late or out of order. VS Code layers: tasks.json builds ( gcc -g … ); launch.json runs the result under GDB via the cppdbg adapter. “Debug with input redirected” launches bash -lc "prog < file" . Test with variety. A buggy line that toggles instead of clears is invisible on inputs where the bit already had the right value. Choose inputs that make the intended and buggy behaviors differ. Common trap: Believing the breakpoint line has already run when it pauses. It has not. Common trap: Trusting passing tests that all share one property (e.g. every test starts with the bit already set). Common trap: Debugging by random edits instead of predicting values and finding the first divergence. Common trap: Assuming printf output appears immediately. Without a newline or fflush it may not. Common trap: Forgetting -g : without debug symbols the debugger cannot map machine code back to your lines and variables.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: Where does a breakpoint pause? — Before its line executes.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: Step Over vs Step Into vs Step Out? — Over: run this line (and any call it makes) as one step. Into: pause on the first line inside the called function. Out: run until the current function returns.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: Why does the Variables panel show c = 97 for an int c holding ‘a’? — It displays by declared type. Add a Watch like (char)c to see the character.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: When is stdout flushed? — On a newline (to a terminal), when the buffer fills, on fflush(stdout) , or when the program exits.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: Why can stderr output appear before earlier stdout output? — stderr is unbuffered but stdout is buffered, especially when piped or redirected, so stdout waits for a flush.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: What does tasks.json do vs launch.json ? — tasks.json defines the build ( gcc -g … ). launch.json defines how to run it under the debugger (cppdbg → GDB), including the preLaunchTask that triggers the build.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: What does the -g flag do? — Includes debug symbols so the debugger can show source lines and variable names.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: How does “Debug with input redirected” work? — It launches /bin/bash -lc "prog < file" so bash redirects stdin from the file, then runs your program.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: The debugging loop in one line? — Predict what each variable should be, step line by line, find the first line where actual differs from predicted, fix, then rerun all tests.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: Why can a buggy function pass some tests? — If the buggy operation and the correct one agree on those inputs (e.g. toggle vs clear when the bit is already 1). Choose inputs where they differ.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: What is a watch expression for? — Monitoring a variable or computed expression (including casts or hex format) as you step.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: The debugger stops at a breakpoint on the line x = x + 1; . Has that line executed? — You inspect the state before the line, then step to see its effect.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: The paused line is result = square(7); . What do Step Over and Step Into do? — Use Into when you suspect the function body, Over when you trust it.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: After int c = getchar(); reads the letter a, the Variables panel shows c = 97 . How do you see 'a' ? — The panel shows by declared type (int, decimal). A cast in Watch reinterprets the bits.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: Which VS Code file defines the gcc command that builds your program before debugging? — tasks.json builds, launch.json runs (and points at the build with preLaunchTask).

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: When does text written with printf to a terminal actually get sent out? Select all that apply. — Output is buffered until one of those events happens.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: This function has a bug (it should clear bit 1 but uses XOR). What does each call return? int modify(int x) { x = x | (1 << 3); // set bit 3 x = x ^ (1 << 2); // toggle bit 2 x = x ^ (1 << 1); // BUG: meant "clear bit 1" x = x | 1; // set bit 0 return x; } — modify(2) and modify(6) have bit 1 already set, so the buggy XOR happens to clear it and they pass (expected 13 and 9). modify(0) has bit 1 clear, so XOR sets it: 15 instead of the intended 13.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: You set a breakpoint and watch s and i . Fill in the values at each moment. int s = 0; for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) { s += i * i; } — s accumulates 1, 4, 9, 16: after i = 3 it is 14; after i = 4 it is 30. The loop exits when i++ makes i equal to 5 and the test i <= 4 fails.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: The program reads the three characters a , Z , 1 . Each is uppercased if it is lowercase. Fill in the value of c (decimal, as the Variables panel shows) after the if block for each. while ((c = getchar()) != EOF) { if (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') { c = c - ('a' - 'A'); } putchar(c); } — 'a' (97) is lowercase, so it drops by 32 to 65. 'Z' (90) is not lowercase and stays 90. '1' (49) is not a letter and stays 49.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: This function should set bit 4, clear bit 2, toggle bit 0 . It returns the wrong value for some inputs. Find the root cause. — Clear with AND and an inverted mask: x = x & ~(1 << 2); .

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: A function that should clear bit 2 uses x ^ (1 << 2) by mistake. Which single test input exposes the bug? — XOR and “clear” only disagree when the bit starts at 0. Good test inputs make the buggy and correct behavior differ.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: Fill the debugger-friendly build flag, and the operator that feeds a file to the program’s stdin. gcc __0__ main.c -o main ./main __1__ test.txt — -g adds debug symbols. < redirects stdin from the file (what the “debug with input redirected” configuration does through bash).

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: While stepping through a loop, characters from putchar(c) do not show up until the program ends. What is the most direct fix? — fflush forces the buffer out right now, so each character appears as you step.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: Put the steps of a disciplined debugging session in order. Two steps are bad habits. — Reproduce, predict, step, find the first divergence, fix, and re-test everything. Random edits and blanket printfs skip the reasoning that finds the actual cause.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: You step over c = c & ~0x20; with int c = 'a'; and watch c and (char)c . Fill in what each shows. int c = 'a'; c = c & ~0x20; — 'a' is 0b0110_0001. Clearing bit 5 (0x20) gives 0b0100_0001 = 65 = 'A'. The Variables panel shows the int in decimal; the cast in Watch shows the character. (Clearing bit 5 uppercases ASCII letters.)

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: The program p does printf("out\n"); then fprintf(stderr, "err\n"); . Both streams go into a pipe with ./p 2>&1 | cat . In what order do the lines come out? — stderr is unbuffered, so err is written immediately. stdout going to a pipe is fully buffered, so out sits in memory until the program exits. This is exactly the kind of surprise that makes output ordering unreliable when debugging with prints.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: A program prints the right numbers for small inputs but a wrong total for one large input. You have the source. Which approach finds the bug fastest and teaches you the most? — A prediction gives you something to compare against, and stepping finds the first place reality departs from it.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: You wrote int8_t set_bit(int8_t num, int8_t i) . List at least five test cases (inputs and expected outputs) and say what each one is designed to catch. — Examples: • set_bit(0, 0) = 1 : lowest bit • set_bit(0, 6) = 64 : a high bit • set_bit(10, 1) = 10 : bit already set, must stay unchanged (catches toggle/XOR bugs) • set_bit(8, 0) = 9 : leaves other bits alone • set_bit(12, 4) = 28 : mixed pattern • i = 7 : sign bit edge case for int8_t The most important property: include cases where the bit is already set and where it is not .

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: A function average(int *a, int n) returns a wrong value only when the array has more than 4 elements. Describe, step by step, how you would find the bug using the VS Code debugger (not by guessing). — 1. Reproduce with the smallest failing input (5 elements) and note actual vs expected. 2. Predict by hand the running sum and each variable after every iteration. 3. Build with -g , set a breakpoint before the loop, add Watch expressions for the sum, the index and the array elements. 4. Step line by line (Step Over the calls you trust) and compare each value to the prediction. 5. Stop at the first line where the value differs. Form a hypothesis about why, fix it, and rerun all tests, including the small ones.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: Explain why output from printf may appear late, or in a different order from fprintf(stderr, ...) , and what you can do about it. — The C library collects stdout writes in a buffer for efficiency and only sends them at flush events. stderr skips buffering so errors show instantly. When both go to one place, ordering can differ from the order of the calls.

title: Mastery: Debugging
text: Describe how VS Code, tasks.json, launch.json, cppdbg and GDB fit together when you press the debug button, and how “debug with input redirected” differs. — Pressing debug runs the build task (gcc -g), then starts GDB through cppdbg with the program. The redirected configuration wraps the program in a bash command so stdin comes from a file.

title: Mastery: Putting it together (cross-topic)
text: Exam-style problems where several ideas interact: types and bitwise inside stack frames, shell streams around a C program, debugging a number-representation bug. Practice choosing the right idea when nothing tells you which one to use. Name the lens for every value. What type is it, how many bits, signed or unsigned, a copy or an address? Most wrong answers come from the wrong lens. Draw the memory. Sketch each frame (RA, params, locals) and the arrays they share. Mark which cells are copies and which are addresses back to a caller . Execute one line at a time and write the value of every variable after each line. Do not skip to the answer. Check the edges: overflow and wraparound at the type’s width, off-by-one on array bounds, the null terminator, signed vs unsigned shifts. Know who does what: the shell (expansion, redirection, PATH), the C program (streams, buffers), the debugger (breakpoints, watches). A question often asks you to trace across all three. When two answers look possible, run a tiny case by hand (size 1 or 2, value 0 or −1) to separate them. Common trap: Solving the last concept first and ignoring a wraparound or copy that happened earlier. Common trap: Reading int8_t / uint8_t arithmetic as if it stayed in 8 bits. Operands are promoted to int ; the wrap happens when you store back. Common trap: Forgetting that the shell sets up redirection before the program starts, and that pipes carry only stdout. Common trap: An unsigned loop counter that counts down to ≥ 0 never ends. Common trap: Mixing up “the value” and “where it lives” when a pointer is involved.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: The five-step plan for a multi-concept code question? — 1) Name each value’s type/width/sign and copy-vs-address. 2) Draw frames and shared arrays. 3) Execute line by line, writing every value. 4) Check wraparound, bounds, null terminator. 5) Test a tiny case by hand.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: Why does a countdown loop for (unsigned char i = 10; i >= 0; i--) never end? — Unsigned values cannot go below 0: after 0, i-- wraps to 255, so i >= 0 is always true.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: int8_t arithmetic: when does it wrap? — Operands are promoted to int for the math; the wrap happens when the result is stored back into the 8-bit variable.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: Where does redirection happen, and what does a pipe carry? — The shell sets it up before the program starts. A pipe carries only stdout; stderr goes to the terminal unless you use 2>&1 .

title: Mastery: Integration
text: Flip the case of an ASCII letter with one bit operation? — XOR with 0x20 toggles case. & ~0x20 forces uppercase, | 0x20 forces lowercase (letters only).

title: Mastery: Integration
text: Why is pack(int8_t r, int8_t g, int8_t b) a bug for byte colors? — A signed value ≥ 128 is negative; promotion sign-extends it and the 1 bits overwrite the other channels. Use uint8_t (zero extension).

title: Mastery: Integration
text: Why is s[strlen(s) - 1] = '\0' dangerous? — For the empty string, strlen is 0 and the unsigned subtraction wraps to a huge index (out-of-bounds write).

title: Mastery: Integration
text: Set a bit through a pointer parameter? — void f(uint8_t *p, int i) { *p |= (1 << i); } called as f(&x, 3) .

title: Mastery: Integration
text: Two’s complement negate via a pointer? — *p = ~*p + 1; (and remember −128 negates to itself).

title: Mastery: Integration
text: The same 8 bits can be 200, −56, or a character. What decides? — The type you read them as: uint8_t , int8_t , or char with %c . The bits never change.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: Fill in each result. char a = 'A' ^ 0x20; char b = 'q' & ~0x20; int n = '7' ^ 0x20; printf("%c %c %d", a, b, n); — 0x20 is the case bit. Toggling it turns 'A' into 'a'; clearing it turns 'q' into 'Q'. For the digit '7' (0x37), XOR 0x20 gives 0x17 = 23, which is not a printable letter: this trick is for letters only.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: The same data, summed into a narrow and into a wide variable. Fill in both. int8_t v[3] = {100, 100, 100}; int32_t wide = 0; int8_t narrow = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { wide += v[i]; narrow += v[i]; } — wide holds the true sum, 300. narrow wraps every time it is stored: 100, then 200 → −56, then −56 + 100 = 44 (equivalently 300 − 256). The width of the accumulator decides.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: Fill in the final state. Track both the array and the pointer. int32_t a[3] = {5, 6, 7}; int32_t *p = a + 1; *p += 10; p++; *p *= 2; — a + 1 points at a[1]; *p += 10 makes it 16. p++ moves to a[2], which doubles to 14. The pointer difference p - a is 2 elements.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: The program count prints the number of digit characters on stdout and prints skip on stderr for every other character except newline. After ./count < in.txt > out.txt 2> err.txt with in.txt containing a1b22 , fill in: — The digits are 1, 2, 2 (3). The non-digits are ‘a’ and ‘b’ (2 skip lines). The shell wires stdin to in.txt, stdout to out.txt and stderr to err.txt before the program starts, so nothing prints on the terminal.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: The program asc prints the decimal value of each input character, one per line. What does printf 'Hi\n' | ./asc | tr '\n' ' ' print? — ‘H’ is 72, ‘i’ is 105, and the newline that printf appends is character 10. tr then joins the lines with spaces.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: What does this print? (three numbers separated by spaces) int8_t x = -8; uint8_t y = x; printf("%d %d %d", x >> 1, y >> 1, (int8_t)(y << 1)); — x >> 1 is an arithmetic shift of 1111_1000: 1111_1100 = −4. y holds the same bits as 248, so y >> 1 is a logical shift: 0111_1100 = 124. y << 1 is 496 in int; narrowing to int8_t keeps the low 8 bits (1111_0000) = −16.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: pack(0x10, 0xC8, 0x20) should return 0x10C820 but returns 0xFFFFC820 . Which line is the root cause? — Use uint8_t so each channel is zero-extended. Signed vs unsigned is a bug source whenever small types are widened.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: This loop is meant to print 10 down to 0, but it never ends. Find the root cause. — Use a signed type for the counter, or test i > 0 and handle 0 separately.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: trim_newline removes the last character of a string. It works on “hello\n” but crashes or corrupts memory on the empty string “”. Which line is the problem? — Check strlen(s) > 0 first. strlen returns an unsigned size_t , so 0 − 1 wraps around.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: This converts one hex digit character to its value and combines two of them. Fill in the results. int hexval(char c) { return c <= '9' ? c - '0' : c - 'A' + 10; } int a = hexval('7'); int b = hexval('B'); int v = hexval('7') * 16 + hexval('B'); — '7' is a digit: 55 − 48 = 7. 'B' is above '9', so 'B' − 'A' + 10 = 11. Two hex digits make a byte: 7 × 16 + 11 = 123 = 0x7B. (ASCII arithmetic, number bases and C expressions in one problem.)

title: Mastery: Integration
text: Fill in each variable after the calls. void negate(int8_t *p) { *p = ~*p + 1; } int main(void) { int8_t a = 5, b = -128, c = 0; negate(&a); negate(&b); negate(&c); } — Flip and add 1 negates 5 to −5. For −128 (1000_0000): flip gives 0111_1111 (127), plus 1 is 128, which does not fit and wraps back to −128. Zero stays zero. The pointer makes each change visible in main.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: Fill in the output pieces. void upcase(char *s) { for (; *s; s++) { if (*s >= 'a' && *s <= 'z') *s -= 32; } } int main(void) { char w[] = "ab1z"; upcase(w); printf("%s %zu", w, strlen(w)); } — upcase walks the pointer until it reaches the null terminator, uppercasing letters in place (the caller’s array changes). '1' is not a lowercase letter and stays. The string is still 4 characters long.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: Across the whole course: select all true statements. — Wraparound at the type width, getchar returning an int (to represent EOF), and bitwise AND of 101 and 010 are true. The others confuse decay, stream numbers, and export.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: Write uint32_t set_channel(uint32_t color, int channel, uint8_t value) that replaces one channel of a packed 0xRRGGBB color (channel 0 = blue, 1 = green, 2 = red) and leaves the others unchanged. Then say why you must clear before you OR. — uint32_t set_channel(uint32_t color, int channel, uint8_t value) { int shift = channel * 8; uint32_t mask = (uint32_t)0xFF << shift; color &= ~mask; // clear the old channel color |= ((uint32_t)value << shift); // write the new one return color; } OR can only turn bits on, so without clearing, old 1 bits in that channel would survive and corrupt the new value. value is unsigned so it zero-extends and cannot spill into other channels.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: Write a C program that reads stdin and prints how many uppercase letters it saw (just the number). Then give the exact shell command that runs it on essay.txt , saves the count to count.txt , and lets error messages still appear on the terminal. — #include <stdio.h> int main(void) { int c, n = 0; while ((c = getchar()) != EOF) { if (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') n++; } printf("%d\n", n); return 0; } ./a.out < essay.txt > count.txt . Stdin comes from the file, stdout goes to count.txt, and stderr is untouched so errors still reach the terminal.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: Walk through what happens when you type ./prog < in.txt > out.txt and prog ’s main calls f(arr) , which prints a result with printf . Cover the shell, the streams and the stack. — The shell sets up the plumbing first. Inside the process, main and f each get a frame; f only receives an address of the array. Output goes through the stdout buffer into out.txt.

title: Mastery: Integration
text: The byte 0xC8 can be 200, −56, the character ‘È’, or part of a color. Explain what decides which one you get, using types, casts, printf and shifts. — Nothing in the byte says what it “is”. The declared type and the format specifier choose the interpretation, and the rules for widening and shifting follow the type.
